contexts.name: Roma - Capitolium - Giardino Romano (funerary)
contexts.description:
The 'Giardino Romano' is the inner courtyard of the Palazzo dei Conservatori (Capitoline Museums), between the Palazzo dei Conservatori and Palazzo Caffarelli, on the southern summit of the Capitoline Hill (the Capitolium proper). Excavations carried out in 1999–2000 for the Sovraintendenza Capitolina, in connection with the new hall of the Museums, exposed large parts of the cappellaccio foundations of the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus and investigated the protohistoric levels beneath them. These yielded the earliest direct evidence of stable occupation of the hill, traces of bronze metallurgy, structural remains from the Recent Bronze Age onwards and a small group of Iron Age burials, whose food offerings were studied by A. Celant and C. Minniti. Finds are displayed in the 'Braccio Nuovo' of the Capitoline Museums.

Bibliography: Celant, A., Minniti, C. 2008. Offerte funerarie alimentari. In Albertoni, M., Damiani, I. (eds), Il tempio di Giove e le origini del colle Capitolino. Milano: Electa: 55–56; Sommella Mura, A. 2009. Il tempio di Giove Capitolino: una nuova proposta di lettura. Annali della Fondazione per il Museo 'Claudio Faina' XVI: 333–372.

contexts.description:

Minniti and published in the exhibition catalogue 'Il tempio di Giove e le origini del colle Capitolino' (2008).

contexts.name: "Sant'Omobono"Sacred Area
contexts.description:
The Sant’Omobono sacred area lies at the foot of the Capitoline Hill, by the Vicus Iugarius and the river-harbour zone of the Forum Boarium, in a topographic setting strongly connected with traffic, exchange, and waterfront activities along the Tiber. 

The site preserves a long stratified sequence: beneath the later temples, investigations documented early occupation and cult traces, while the major monumentalisation is placed around 580 BC, when an Etrusco-Italic temple was built; this building was destroyed at the end of the 6th century BC, and—after a period of neglect—the area was later raised and reconfigured for the better-known sanctuary traditionally identified (from literary sources) with Fortuna and Mater Matuta. 

From an archaeobotanical perspective, the 6th-century contexts published for the sanctuary are characterised in broad terms by charred cereals and fruit crops (notably hulled wheats/barley and Mediterranean orchard/vine taxa), a spectrum consistent with food-related practices that can plausibly include offerings and consumption debris within a cult setting.

contexts.name: Roma - Ss. Quattro Coronati (settlement)
contexts.description:
The Basilica of Santi Quattro Coronati is part of a fortified monastic complex on the Caelian Hill, along the line of an ancient road traditionally identified with the old Via Tuscolana. From Late Antiquity onward the site is thought to occupy the area of a high-status residential property; an apsed hall was converted into a church before 499, when the titulus Aemilianae is first recorded, later associated with Santi Quattro Coronati. 

A major Carolingian reorganisation—credited to Pope Leo IV (847–855)—included fortifications and key structural additions (courtyard/tower system and related service spaces), setting the stage for the later “fortress-like” character of the complex. 

After the 1084 destruction (Norman sack), Pope Paschal II rebuilt the basilica on a reduced footprint and created the distinctive sequence of two courtyards, while the flanking sectors evolved into monastic and cardinal residential spaces. 

Modern restoration campaigns have also produced stratified archaeological evidence (e.g., Roman walls, early-medieval surfaces and medieval construction-yard traces), and early-modern “domestic” bio-assemblages that offer a small window onto diet and provisioning within the complex.

contexts.name: Roma - Centocelle - Area T. 505 (settlement)
contexts.description:
The Centocelle archaeological park, on the south-eastern outskirts of Rome along the Via Casilina, occupies the area of the former 'Francesco Baracca' airfield. Preventive investigations by the Sovraintendenza Capitolina in the 1990s, within the planned Sistema Direzionale Orientale (SDO), documented frequentation since prehistory and three Roman villas: the villa 'ad duas lauros', the 'Villa della Piscina' and the 'Villa delle Terme'. Area T.505 yielded Archaic and early-Republican occupation contexts – channels, ditches and tunnels, and filling deposits – whose plant remains were analysed by F. Larocca and A. Celant.

Bibliography: Gioia, P., Volpe, R. (eds) 2004. Centocelle I. Roma S.D.O. Le indagini archeologiche. Soveria Mannelli: Rubbettino; Volpe, R. (ed.) 2007. Centocelle II. Roma S.D.O. Le indagini archeologiche. Soveria Mannelli: Rubbettino.; Larocca, F., Celant, A. 2004. L'occupazione arcaica e altorepubblicana: risultati delle ricerche archeobotaniche. In Gioia, Volpe (eds) 2004: 287.

contexts.name: Roma - Quadrato di Torre Spaccata (settlement)
contexts.description:
Quadrato di Torre Spaccata is a large prehistoric settlement on the south-eastern edge of Rome, along the former valley margin of the Fosso di Gregna (an ancient tributary of the Aniene). The site was investigated in multiple campaigns: the core area (often referred to as Area A) was excavated in 1981 and 1984–85, while further works connected to the Jubilee 2000 explored the south-eastern edge of the settlement (Sector C), clarifying its extent and internal organisation. 

Neolithic occupation (older phase)

The 1981 and 1984–85 excavations exposed a Late Neolithic occupation surface characterised by very dense pottery scatters and a set of activity features: irregular pits, fired-clay working surfaces, and areas linked to lithic production/working. Archaeobotanical evidence (charred crops and fuel wood) indicates an agricultural component already well established at the site. 

Eneolithic occupation (later phase)

In the Jubilee 2000 sector, Eneolithic structures were found directly overlying the older Neolithic level (partly truncated by erosion). In total, the SE investigations identified two Neolithic huts and three Eneolithic huts, including a larger rectangular structure partly cut by a later Roman paved road; a radiocarbon AMS date from charcoal in a hut foundation gully places the Eneolithic phase broadly in the later 3rd millennium BC. 
Academia

Bibliography: Anzidei & Carboni (eds.) 1995 (Origini XIX); Celant 1995 (in Origini XIX); Anzidei & Carboni 2007 (Jubilee 2000 excavations, Sector C).

Small, isolated pocket of archaeobotanical material plotted separately from the main Areas 1–4, used in the 1995 study to track micro-distribution across the living surface.

contexts.name: Area 3 - small cluster of botanical remains (center)
contexts.description:

contexts.name: T38E - horse and dogs burial
contexts.description: A shallow 'pozzetto' containing a ritually arranged horse burial, with two dog puppies deposited above and sealed by clay. Charcoal from this feature was included in anthracological counts and also used for dating, making it a key anchor point linking botanical evidence to ritualised activity at the settlement margin.

contexts.description:
Occupation surface in the marginal activity zone, where burning/daub concentrations and hearth-related residues were recorded. 

This context probably reflects day-to-day fuel use and woodland catchment activities near the lakeshore settlement.

contexts.name: Anguillara Sabazia La Marmotta (underwater)
contexts.description:
La Marmotta is an Early Neolithic lakeshore village now lying under the waters of Lake Bracciano (Anguillara Sabazia, Rome), on the south-eastern shore near the outflow of the River Arrone. The deposit lies c. 300 m from the modern shoreline at about 11 m below the present lake surface (c. 8 m of water and 3 m of sediment); the settlement covered about 2 ha, of which roughly a quarter was excavated during the underwater campaigns of 1992–2006 directed by M.A. Fugazzola Delpino (Museo Pigorini, now Museo delle Civiltà).

Waterlogging preserved an exceptional organic record: around 3,400 piles supporting the dwellings, wattle-and-daub walls, plant-stem roofs and wooden or bark floors, together with five dugout canoes and navigation-related objects, wooden tools (including over fifty sickles), basketry, cordage and textiles. The stratigraphy comprises three contiguous layers with no sterile interface: Layer II (foundation of the village, Tyrrhenian Impressed Ware), Layer I (the most intense occupation, Cardial and Painted Ware) and the 'Chiocciolaio' layer (abandonment). Radiocarbon dates on posts, poppy seeds and emmer caryopses place the occupation in the second half of the 6th millennium cal BC (c. 7600–7200 cal BP), making La Marmotta one of the earliest farming villages of the central-western Mediterranean.

Bibliography: Mazzucco, N. et al. 2022. "Multiproxy study of 7500-year-old wooden sickles from the Lakeshore Village of La Marmotta, Italy". Scientific Reports 12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-18597-8; Mineo, M. et al. 2023. "Textiles, basketry and cordage from the Early Neolithic settlement of La Marmotta, Lazio". Antiquity 97; Rottoli, M. 1993. Analisi paletnobotaniche: prime risultanze. Appendice 1 in "La Marmotta", Anguillara Sabazia (RM). Scavi 1989. Un abitato perilacustre di età neolitica.

contexts.name: Anguillara Sabazia La Marmotta - Liv. I Sup
contexts.description:
Sampling unit corresponding to the upper part of Layer I ('Livello I superiore') of the submerged Early Neolithic village of La Marmotta. In the site sequence, Layer II marks the foundation of the settlement, while Layer I represents its most intense occupation (Cardial and Painted Ware), sealed by the 'Chiocciolaio' abandonment layer. The plant remains from these levels were among the first published from the site (analyses of the 1989 campaign by M. Rottoli).

contexts.name: Lunghezzina cemetery
contexts.description:
The Eneolithic necropolis of Lunghezzina lies on a tuff plateau sloping west toward the Fosso della Vitellara (a tributary of the Aniene river). It was first identified during large-scale ground stripping connected with modern building works, and investigated through multiple campaigns (starting in 1998). Early excavation reports documented two main clusters of rock-cut graves (a NW nucleus and a SE nucleus, tens of metres apart) plus an isolated burial at greater distance; later syntheses indicate that additional chamber tombs were recognized as fieldwork progressed. 

Most graves belong to the Copper Age tradition of artificial “grotticella” chamber tombs cut into the tuff, typically with a small vestibule and a sub-elliptical burial cell. Repeated reopening/reuse is suggested by disturbed and re-arranged human remains in several tombs, as well as by architectural details such as lateral recesses near the chamber access; in at least one case, charcoal concentrations were interpreted as possible traces of wooden closures.

From an archaeobotanical standpoint, macro-remains at Lunghezzina are mainly charcoal/wood fragments recovered from selected tomb fills and thresholds (notably Tombs 2, 3, 6 and 8), informative both for ritual/technical practices and (in some cases) for radiocarbon dating. 

Bibliography: Anzidei et al., La necropoli eneolitica di Lunghezzina (Roma) (2003); Anzidei e Carboni 2020, "Roma prima del mito".

contexts.name: Lunghezzina cemetery - tomb 3
contexts.description:
Tomb 3 is a chamber tomb cut into the tuff and strongly truncated by ploughing, preserving a shallow chamber and a reduced entrance/threshold zone (with a step/downward transition into the cell). The fill is compact and the anthropolical material is fragmentary: teeth and traces of skeletal remains suggest a young adult, with limited grave goods (small quantities of pottery and lithics). 

Tomb 3 produced charcoal/wood fragments identified as alder (Alnus) and maple (Acer). A separate radiocarbon measurement is reported from an oak (Quercus) charcoal sample taken from this tomb (OxA-8078: 3990±55 BP; cal. 2720–2490 BC), linking Tomb 3 securely to the later 3rd millennium BC (Copper Age).

Bibliography: Anzidei et al., La necropoli eneolitica di Lunghezzina (Roma) (2003); Anzidei e Carboni 2020, "Roma prima del mito".

contexts.name: Lunghezzina cemetery - tomb 8
contexts.description:
In the Lunghezzina cemetery, Tomb 8 stands out for its preservation and stratigraphic potential. It is a chamber tomb with part of the vault surviving, and a vestibule described as semi-lunar and sloping toward the chamber. The structure yielded clear evidence relevant to closure practices and “threshold activity” (including a flint arrowhead interpreted as a possible offering), while differences in sediment between vestibule and chamber were used to argue for controlled access and possible periodic reopening.

It is also the richest context for charcoal macro-remains: anthracological analysis reports ash (Fraxinus sp.) as dominant (dozens of fragments from the cell/vestibule/near the recesses), along with maple (Acer sp.) from the chamber floor and alder (Alnus sp.) from the vestibule. A radiocarbon determination is reported from an ash charcoal sample connected with the door/recess area (LTL2901A: 4100±60 BP; cal. 2890–2620 BC).

Bibliography: Anzidei et al., La necropoli eneolitica di Lunghezzina (Roma) (2003); Anzidei e Carboni 2020, "Roma prima del mito".

contexts.name: Lunghezzina cemetery - tomb 6
contexts.description:
Tomb 6 is a relatively better-defined grotticella tomb, with a sub-rectangular vestibule and lateral recesses near the chamber access. Small travertine stones found near the entrance are interpreted not as door-slabs but more plausibly as markers/ritual elements. The chamber yielded little or no in situ human skeletal material in the excavated levels; finds from the fill include small artefacts such as a copper awl, consistent with a funerary assemblage but not particularly rich. 

Botanical macro-remains are especially meaningful here; tomb 6 produced seven charcoal fragments of elm (Ulmus sp.), concentrated in the left lateral recess close to the chamber entrance—a pattern explicitly interpreted as possibly related to a wooden closing device/door rather than casual background charcoal.

Bibliography: Anzidei et al., La necropoli eneolitica di Lunghezzina (Roma) (2003); Anzidei e Carboni 2020, "Roma prima del mito".

contexts.name: Montalto di Castro - Chiesa di San Sisto (funerary)
contexts.site: Montalto di Castro - Chiesa di San Sisto
contexts.description:
The church of San Sisto forms part of an extra-moenia complex along the road linking Montalto di Castro with its coastal hamlet. Built in the later Middle Ages (commonly placed in the late 13th century) and tied to monastic life, the complex was later transformed for public-health and assistance purposes: it functioned as a lazaretto and then as a hospital in the early modern period (with major 18th-century alterations), and today it is reused as a venue for cultural activities/events.

Archaeological excavations carried out in 2000-2001 exposed a funerary phase on the earlier cocciopesto walking level: a rock-cut crypt (Tomb 1) near the entrance, additional ossuaries, and a set of small pit-type graves (Graves 3–7) cut through the floor and reused over time. These data show that, alongside its liturgical role, the building (or parts of it) served as a burial space between the 15th–16th centuries and into the post-medieval period.

Bibliography: Sadori e Sabato 2009

contexts.name: grave 3
contexts.site: Montalto di Castro - Chiesa di San Sisto
contexts.description:
Grave 3 belongs to the group of small pit-type graves (3–7) cut into the cocciopesto floor after the main hypogeal/ossuary phase. Grave 3 itself was found intact at discovery and contained multiple inhumations (an adult female c. 20–30 years and two infants), with small personal/devotional items (e.g., textile fragments, rosary parts, a bronze earring, a gold enamelled ring).

The botanical evidence derives primarily from coffin construction: wood traces preserved by “metallization” around iron nails, identified as alder (Alnus sp.), with plank thickness inferred at c. 25–28 mm.

Bibliography: Sadori e Sabato 2009

contexts.name: grave 6
contexts.site: Montalto di Castro - Chiesa di San Sisto
contexts.description:
Grave 6 belongs to the group of small pit-type graves (3–7) cut into the cocciopesto floor after the main hypogeal/ossuary phase. The grave was repeatedly reopened/reused. The final use of Grave 6, along with other tombs of this group, is connected to a phase of repairs/patching in the western aisle (bricks used to plug lacunae), after which a thin cocciopesto layer sealed some graves.

Archaeobotanical evidence comes from the coffin construction: Grave 6 is explicitly grouped with Graves 3 and 5 for the wooden remains preserved on nails, all identified as alder (Alnus sp.), again with consistent board thickness inferred from the nail-associated traces.

Bibliography: Sadori e Sabato 2009

contexts.name: Lago di Mezzano (underwater)
contexts.description:
Lago di Mezzano is a small volcanic lake within the Latera caldera (Valentano, Viterbo). Two submerged lake-dwelling settlements were discovered on its bottom in 1972; after a first survey (1973) and underwater excavations (1975), research continued in 1983–1996 under P. Petitti (Soprintendenza per l'Etruria meridionale). Material concentrates in three areas: M1 in front of the outflow of the Olpeta, M3 on the northern shore close to M1, and M2 on the eastern shore.

A substantial occupation begins in the advanced Early Bronze Age and continues through the early Middle Bronze Age, when the settlement reached its greatest extent; it then contracted, and the Recent Bronze Age is documented mainly by exceptional bronzes, including swords interpreted as votive depositions. Wooden piles and planks recovered in 1973 were identified by M. Follieri and A. Catullo and dated by radiocarbon at the University of Rome; pollen cores taken in 1995 show human impact (cultivated plants, forest clearance and possible pasture).

Bibliography: Follieri, M., Coccolini, G.B.L., Catullo, A. 1976. Strutture lignee di un abitato dell'età del Bronzo nel lago di Mezzano (Viterbo). Annali di Botanica 35: 175–183; Alessio, M. et al. 1975. University of Rome Carbon-14 Dates XIII. Radiocarbon 17(3): 313–327; Catalogo Generale dei Beni Culturali (ICCD), scheda MA 'Lago di Mezzano' (ICCD13695561).

contexts.name: Lago di Bolsena - Gran Carro (underwater)
contexts.description:
The 'Gran Carro' is a submerged protohistoric settlement on the eastern shore of Lake Bolsena (loc. S. Antonio, Bolsena, Viterbo). Discovered in 1959 by A. Fioravanti, it was investigated underwater by the Soprintendenza from the 1960s to the late 1980s (from the mid-1980s also by the team of the Museo Territoriale del Lago di Bolsena) and research resumed in 2012. The remains lie on a lakebed sloping down to c. 7.5 m, about 100 m from the present shore, over c. 1.5 ha.

The site was founded in the Middle Bronze Age (15th century BC), but its most substantial remains belong to the Early Iron Age (late 10th–9th century BC, Villanovan). More than 450 wooden piles are arranged in parallel bands about 3 m apart (NE–SW), together with wall and roofing elements, hearths, loom remains, storage vessels and bronzes; cultural layers up to 160 cm thick record repeated levelling and fires, and rising lake levels eventually led to the relocation of houses and abandonment. An elliptical stone structure (the 'Aiola') is interpreted as an open-air ritual place active from at least the 11th century BC. Archaeobotanical studies range from the 1980s (Costantini & Costantini Biasini 1987; Hopf & Tamburini 1995) to the analysis of charred cereals and millets inside pottery vessels (Fundurulic et al. 2022).

Bibliography: Tamburini, P. (ed.) 1995. Un abitato villanoviano perilacustre. Il "Gran Carro" sul lago di Bolsena (1959–1985). Roma; Fundurulic, A. et al. 2022. "Millets and Cereal Meals from the Early Iron Age Underwater Settlement of 'Gran Carro' (Bolsena Lake, Central Italy)". Sustainability 14(7): 3941. https://doi.org/10.3390/su14073941; Barbaro, B., Severi, E. 2020. L'abitato sommerso della prima età del Ferro del Gran Carro di Bolsena: verso una nuova prospettiva. Analysis Archaeologica 4: 25–51.

contexts.name: Vessel 3 -XI Bc.
contexts.description:
Pottery vessel no. 3 from the 1980 underwater excavation at the Gran Carro, whose plant content was determined by M. Hopf (Hopf & Tamburini 1995); the source attributes it to the 11th century BC. Vessels with charred food remains are among the most informative contexts of the submerged settlement, where finds were recovered from collapsed occupation layers.

contexts.name: Tarquinia
contexts.description:
The Civita plateau of Tarquinia hosted the Etruscan city of Tarchna. The so-called 'complesso monumentale' on the Pian di Civita has been excavated systematically since 1982 by the Università degli Studi di Milano (Progetto Tarquinia, directed by M. Bonghi Jovino and, from 2005, by G. Bagnasco Gianni), after the earlier work of P. Romanelli (1934–1938, 1946) and the Lerici geophysical prospections.

The complex grew around a central sacred area already marked in Proto-Villanovan times (10th century BC) and was progressively expanded towards the west through the Orientalising and Archaic periods (areas alpha, beta and gamma), with building phases that preserved its sacred character. The excavations documented pits and post holes, ritual depositions of vessels and food offerings, foundation deposits, infant burials and the mid-8th-century 'man of the sea' interpreted as a human sacrifice; archaeobotanical analyses have accompanied the excavation since the 1980s (Castelletti 1986; Bedini et al. 1997; Rottoli 2001, 2005). Contexts from the coastal emporic sanctuary of Gravisca, Tarquinia's harbour c. 10 km from the city, are also grouped here.

Bibliography: Bonghi Jovino, M., Chiaramonte Treré, C. (eds) 1997. Tarquinia. Testimonianze archeologiche e ricostruzione storica. Scavi sistematici nell'abitato, campagne 1982–1988 (Tarchna I). Roma; Bedini, E., Rottoli, M., Fornaciari, G., Mallegni, F., Liborio, G. 1997. Analisi di laboratorio. In Bonghi Jovino, Chiaramonte Treré (eds) 1997: 91–144.; Bagnasco Gianni, G. 2021. Tarquinii. Oxford Classical Dictionary.

contexts.name: Tarquinia - Palazzo Vitelleschi (settlement)
contexts.description:
"Palazzo Vitelleschi” occupies a pivotal node in Tarquinia’s historic centre (medieval Corneto) and forms a stratified palimpsest. The 15th-century palace visible today—promoted by Cardinal Giovanni (Maria) Vitelleschi and built mainly in the first half of the fifteenth century—incorporates and reuses late-medieval pre-existing buildings, whose irregular plan strongly conditioned the final layout of the Renaissance complex.

Archaeological work documented both standing medieval fabric and subfloor stratigraphy, effectively preserving a “fossilised” corner of the medieval town within the later palace. In the north-western sector (Area D), a “proto-palace” developed through several phases between the 12th century (when only the tower was present) and the 15th century. Behind this area there is now a corridor connecting to the north-eastern sector, which in the medieval phase was occupied by a narrow street parallel to Via Mazzini. This street separated the “proto-palace” from sector A3, interpreted as a long rectangular house (or a row of houses). Beneath the medieval street—abandoned toward the end of the 14th century / beginning of the 15th century—excavators found a cluster of rock-cut pits backfilled with domestic refuse. Some pits appear to have been filled relatively late, while others must have been out of use for decades, since open pits would have obstructed passage along the street. Overall, the filling of these features spans from the second half of the 12th century to the final phase of the street.

The pit deposits contained “everyday” refuse (food debris, broken pottery) but also an exceptional concentration of intact vessels, personal objects (coins, seals, luxury items), and animal carcasses, suggesting a purposeful clearance episode rather than slow, gradual accumulation. The associated assemblage includes both local wares and wide-ranging imports (e.g., from Pisa, Liguria, Spain, North Africa, and the Near East), consistent with Corneto’s role as a port and with the high status of the household occupying the proto-palace. The same deposits also yielded rich archaeobotanical evidence (carbonised and mineralised) and a very large faunal sample.

Bibliography: Clark et al. 1989. "The Food Refuse of an Affluent Urban Household in the Late Fourteenth Century:
Faunal and Botanical Remains from the Palazzo Vitelleschi, Tarquinia (Viterbo)". In: Papers of the British School at Rome , 1989, Vol. 57 (1989), pp. 200-321.

contexts.name: Submerged Well 112 (Pyrgi coast)
contexts.description:
Well 112 is the lower, still-preserved portion of a circular Etruscan well identified on the seabed within the “Pyrgi Sommersa” underwater archaeological map, in the stretch of water between the medieval castle of Santa Severa and the monumental sanctuary. It lies ca. 68 m from the present shoreline and at about 2.5 m water depth, almost in front of the mouth of the Fosso del Caolino. 

Structurally, what survives is a circular stone-and-clay lining: about 70 cm in diameter, with a stone facing ~30 cm thick, preserved for a maximum height of ~35 cm. The lining is made of stones of different sizes (including limestone blocks, trachyte pebbles, and rarer tuffs). Within the well perimeter, materials were found still in situ in a dark, clayey fill undergoing erosion; recovery required excavating the muddy deposit for roughly 30–35 cm. The fill contained an assemblage of ceramicslead pieces, animal bones, and wooden artefacts.

Chronologically, the well was likely built/used in the Late Etruscan period (possibly 4th c. BC) and closed/filled in Republican times (III/II BC); interpretation remains open between an ordinary water well later filled by accident/intentional dumping and a deliberate “obliteration” (ritual closing) deposit. 

Bibliography: Flavio Enei, Pyrgi sommersa. I risultati delle nuove indagini subacquee, in Annali della Fondazione per il Museo “Claudio Faina” XXV (2018), pp. 347–361; Flavio Enei, Storia e archeologia dei porti ceretani di Pyrgi e Castrum Novum alla luce delle recenti scoperte, in Il Mediterraneo e la Storia II. Seamen, Ports and Navigation (Acta Instituti Romani Finlandiae 45), 2017 (estratto), pp. 234–244.

contexts.name: Well's upper layer
contexts.description:
Upper layer of the dark clayey fill preserved inside the circular stone lining of Well 112, on the seabed off Pyrgi (Santa Severa). The fill, recovered by excavating the eroding muddy deposit for about 30–35 cm, contained an assemblage of ceramics, lead pieces, animal bones and wooden artefacts; its sediment was the object of a pilot archaeobotanical analysis (Kodýdková et al. 2013).

Bibliography: Kodýdková, K., Beneš, J., Komárková, V., Paclíková, K. 2013. Pilot archaeobotanical analysis of the sediment of the well 112 in Pyrgi, Santa Severa. Archaeologia Maritima Mediterranea 10: 181–190; Flavio Enei, Pyrgi sommersa. I risultati delle nuove indagini subacquee, in Annali della Fondazione per il Museo “Claudio Faina” XXV (2018), pp. 347–361; Flavio Enei, Storia e archeologia dei porti ceretani di Pyrgi e Castrum Novum alla luce delle recenti scoperte, in Il Mediterraneo e la Storia II. contexts.name: Vessel B
contexts.description:
In the well’s eroding fill, the standout artefact is a Greco-Italic amphora. It is described as a likely Magna-Graecian or Sicilian product, close to form MGS III, but unusually small for the type: H. 29.5 cm, internal rim diameter 8 cm. It was reconstructable almost entirely from numerous fragments.

contexts.name: Luni sul Mignone (settlemnt)
contexts.description:
Luni sul Mignone is a tuff plateau c. 550 m long and 140 m wide in the comune of Blera (Viterbo), about 65 km north-west of Rome, bounded by steep slopes above the River Mignone, the ancient frontier between Tarquinia and Caere. The Swedish Institute of Classical Studies in Rome, with the Soprintendenza per l'Etruria meridionale, excavated the site from 1960 to 1963 under C.E. Östenberg, also exploring the Tre Erici depression and the surrounding necropoleis.

The site is renowned for its unusual rock-cut house trenches interpreted as Bronze Age 'longhouses' (Middle–Recent Bronze Age, 17th–11th centuries BC), for a monumental, probably two-storey building of the Final Bronze Age–Early Iron Age (Tolfa-Allumiere facies) and for Iron Age huts on the acropolis; later Etruscan, Roman and medieval phases are also attested. Plant remains from the Bronze and Iron Age deposits were studied by H. Helbaek.

Bibliography: Östenberg, C.E. 1967. Luni sul Mignone e problemi della preistoria d'Italia (ActaRom-4°, 25). Lund; Helbaek 1976 (plant remains, as cited in the dataset); Costantini, L. 2002. Italia centro-meridionale. In Forni, G., Marcone, A. (eds), Storia dell'agricoltura italiana I: 221–233.

contexts.name: Stagno - Pratini dell'Argin Traverso (settlement)
contexts.description:
In 1984, a group of speleologists from the Rome section of the Italian Alpine Club (C.A.I.) discovered and reported the presence of ceramic fragments in chambers B, C, D, and E of Grotta dello Sventatoio. A subsequent inspection made it possible to systematically collect all the material found on the surface, leading to the identification of about 8,000 coarse-ware ceramic sherds, belonging to at least 400 vessels. 

In addition to the pottery, a number of bronze objects, bone and stone artefacts, faunal remains, and some human bones of infants were recovered. Several vessels, found almost intact, contained seeds of wheat, barley, and broad beans. The finds indicate that the cave, used as a cult place, was frequented throughout the entire Middle Bronze Age.

(description taken from: https://sabinasacra.lad-sapienza.it/monumento/?tb=luogo_di_interesse&id=434 ; author: L. Alessandri - persional tradution)

Selva dei Muli (settlement)
contexts.description:
At Selva dei Muli, on the northeastern slope of the small volcanic cone, preventive excavations uncovered a portion of a Copper Age (Eneolithic) village attributed to the Gaudo facies. The investigated area covers roughly 4 hectares and revealed an impressive defensive complex consisting of a ditch and at least one palisade, enclosing residential and ancillary structures as well as activity areas.

Based on the data collected, the village appears to have had two phases of stable occupation: the first belongs to an early phase of the Gaudo facies (3120–3010 BC); the second reflects use of the area after the settlement’s abandonment, assignable to the fully Eneolithic phase associated with the Laterza facies (2820–2660 BC). The presence of artifacts such as net weights, spindle whorls, querns and handstones, and flint tools, together with structures interpreted as livestock shelters, suggests a diversified subsistence strategy involving fishing, cultivation, animal husbandry, and perhaps hunting. Moreover, the discovery of three pieces of obsidian originating from Lipari and Palmarola points to a network of long-distance contacts.

Source: MOSI record ID SABAP-LAZ_FR_2020_D810_001, author Pagliarosi, Davide (content manager: Pagliarosi, Davide), compiled in 2022, https://gna.cultura.gov.it (original in Italian; personal translation).

contexts.name: Casale Nuovo (settlement)
contexts.description:
Casale Nuovo is a protohistoric settlement in the province of Latina (southern Latium), a key site for the later Bronze Age of the region, where pottery of Mycenaean type attests Aegean contacts. Plant remains from the site were included in the synthesis of the agricultural economy of Latium south of the Tiber between the Early and Middle Bronze Age by L. Costantini and L. Costantini Biasini (2007).

Bibliography: Angle, M., Caneva, C., Conti, A.M. Casale Nuovo (LT) e la tarda età del bronzo nel Lazio meridionale. In La Sardegna nel Mediterraneo tra il Bronzo Medio e il Bronzo Recente (XVI–XIII sec. a.C.). Atti del III Convegno di studi, Selargius 1987: 265–303; Costantini, L., Costantini Biasini, L. 2007. Economia agricola del Lazio a sud del Tevere tra Bronzo antico e Bronzo medio. Atti XL Riunione Scientifica IIPP: 787–801.

contexts.name: Western Sector - large dump pit
contexts.description:
Area over roughly 100 m² centered on a large pit whose fills include deposits dated to the 13th century BC. This feature was later re-cut and accompanied by a dump pit, additional pits, and small channels, with later phases extending into the Final Bronze Age. Assemblages from the earlier fills include refined (purified) clay pottery, a copper “cake”/ingot fragment and copper (and lead-related) melting residues, a small number of glass-paste beads, and—crucially—an Aegean-type stirrup-jar handle attributed to Late Helladic IIIB–IIIC, suggesting long-distance connections (with provenance discussed through archaeometric sampling in subsequent work).Published plans exist but do not precisely locate the layout within the overall hill setting; the plan is therefore placed here only approximately (as “W”), while preserving correct dimensions. 

Bibliography: Angle et al. 1993, Casale Nuovo (LT) e la tarda età del bronzo nel Lazio meridionale, pp. 273–274; Alessandri, L. 2008, p. 108

contexts.name: Eastern Sector - Final Bronze Age's pit
contexts.description:
Fieldwork in this area documented c. 25 circular pits on the summit and upper slopes, ranging from small features (c. 50–80 cm in diameter) to larger ones (up to c. 150–200 cm), generally shallow in preserved depth beneath the plough zone. Their fills included ceramics (including “Boschetto”-style decorated cups), calcined animal bone, and blocks of light/reddish sandstone interpreted as tempering material, alongside evidence consistent with craft waste. On this basis, the pits have been interpreted as installations for clay settling/decantation connected with nearby clay sources and ceramic production; minor metallurgical indicators (e.g., copper slag and lead) are also reported from the broader area. All archeobotanical materials comes from one such pit.

The published plans (e.g., Tavv. V–VI) provide the pit layouts but lack a precise georeferenced placement on the hillock; therefore, they are positioned only approximately here (following the E/W distinction) while keeping their internal dimensions correct.

Published plans exist but do not precisely locate the layout within the overall hill setting; the plan is therefore placed here only approximately, while preserving correct dimensions. 

Bibliography: Angle et al. 1993, Casale Nuovo (LT) e la tarda età del bronzo nel Lazio meridionale, pp. 272–273; Alessandri, L. 2008, p. 108

contexts.name: Sezze - Grotta Vittorio Vecchi (settlement)
contexts.description: Grotta Vittorio Vecchi is a karst cave on the southern flank of Monte Fulcino (near Sezze Romano, LT), discovered in 1987 by speleologists after the recognition of pottery and metal finds mixed with human skeletal remains. The cave develops along intersecting fractures and, beyond a steep access passage, opens into a sequence of chambers and niches (including the “Sala Appenninica”, the “Strettoia degli Scheletri”, and the “Sala dei Sette”). Two excavation campaigns (1988 and 1989), preceded by systematic surface mapping and gridding, documented the cave’s primary use as a funerary context with associated ritual activity, broadly dating to the late phase of the Early Bronze Age through the Middle Bronze Age; the assemblage included numerous human remains (with a significant infant component) and abundant carbonised botanical remains alongside pottery and occasional metal objects. Bibliography: Guidi & Rosini, Materiali protostorici dalla grotta Vittorio Vecchi (Sezze Romano, LT).NULL

contexts.name: "Sala dei Sette" and A1-3 trenches
contexts.sourceDating: fine del Bronzo antico e il Bronzo medio
contexts.description:
The “Sala dei Sette” is the largest, most accessible chamber in the inner sector of Grotta Vittorio Vecchi and was therefore chosen for stratigraphic investigation. It is a spacious room with niches and dense concentrations of archaeological material, terminating against a major collapse that sealed the ancient entrance. The evidence points to repeated funerary and ritual use, with human remains often clustered along walls and in niches, occasional reworking of older deposits toward the centre, and the presence of a hearth linked to these practices. Fieldwork in and around the chamber was organised through test pits: A2, a long trench along the entrance/collapse, documented a sequence from landslide sealing and water-laid silts to stalagmitic phases and a dark anthropogenic layer rich in Bronze Age materials; A1 sampled this deposit (two spits), yielding later disturbance (including an Archaic bronze fibula) and a hearth above, and denser human remains below (including an inverted bowl covering a child’s skull); A3, between the collapse base and Ambiente A, produced well-preserved pottery (mostly closed forms) and bronze items (e.g., chisel, pin), while Ambiente A yielded in situ bones and the site’s only bronze dagger. Published plans and sections locate the chamber and pits, but as cave-survey drawings without precise georeferencing; GIS placement is therefore approximate, while preserving correct internal proportions. 

Bibliography: Guidi & Rosini, Materiali protostorici dalla grotta Vittorio Vecchi (Sezze Romano, LT).

contexts.name: Privernum - Domus della Soglia Nilotica (settlement)
contexts.description:
Privernum was a rich Roman colony c. 70 km south-east of Rome (Priverno, Latina). Archaeobotanical investigations focused on the garden and related structures of the luxury Domus della Soglia Nilotica, archaeologically and radiocarbon-dated to the second half of the 1st century AD. In the fill of the euripus, the ornamental water basin of the garden, a charred basket woven with Ampelodesmos leaves contained stone-pine seeds and cone scales and peach stones; sediments from the drainage system and the kitchen were processed for macro- and microremains.

Bibliography: Sadori, L., Giardini, M., Susanna, F. 2010. The plant landscape as inferred from a basket of the Roman town of Privernum (Latium, central Italy). Plant Biosystems 144(4): 874–887. https://doi.org/10.1080/11263504.2010.491981

contexts.name: Rieti - Cures Sabini (settlement)
contexts.description:
Cures Sabini, near Fara in Sabina (Rieti), is the Sabine centre traditionally regarded as the homeland of Titus Tatius. Excavations by the Soprintendenza per il Lazio from 1979 (A. Guidi) showed that the settlement began in the early 8th century BC on the western hill, where over 1.5 ha were enclosed by two defensive ditches; from the end of the 8th century it expanded to the hills of Casino d'Arci and S. Maria degli Arci, reaching 25–30 ha in the 7th century. Huts and structures of the 8th–7th century BC were excavated, among them a hut reconstructed in the Museo Civico Archeologico of Fara in Sabina.

Bibliography: Guidi, A. et al. 1987. Cures Sabini: risultati della quinta campagna di scavo. QuadAEI 14: 521–532; Costantini, L., Costantini Biasini, L. 1988. Paleoetnobotanica – nota preliminare. In Cures Sabini: risultati della sesta campagna di scavo. Archeologia Laziale IX (QuadAEI 16): 331–332.

contexts.name: Roma - Viminale (settlement)
contexts.description:
Imperial-age rooms on the Viminal Hill in Rome, including a cryptoporticus, which were reoccupied during the early Middle Ages. Plant remains from these contexts were presented by Masi et al. (2009).

contexts.name: Late Bronze Age - Early Iron Age remains form Caesar's Foro
Ceramic-production complex
contexts.description:
The remains comes from two specific USS:

US 3096: Structural collapse debris from the kiln’s vault/roof associated with the later installation (US 3006); part of the superstructure failure phase (in tandem with US 3069).

US 3007: descrizione Charred elements of the internal wall framework: ash (Fraxinus) planks and members of deciduous oak, belonging to the inner wall framing of the same kiln phase (US 3006).

The ceramic-production complex identified as probable horizontal kilns, set in a sub-elliptical cavity cut into natural silt and clay, with a concave floor sloping east and side walls lined with large tuff blocks. The sequence shows discontinuous use, with phases separated by sandy abandonment fills. The earliest installation (US 3186) was larger and apsidal; it bears a thick carbonaceous layer overlain by sand lenses and “concotto” lumps, plus strongly altered, vitrified, bubble-marked surfaces indicating temperatures >1000 °C (US 3120), likely from an uncontrolled overheating event that led to abandonment. A subsequent, smaller kiln (US 3006), inserted within the first and sharing its orientation, has a thin carbon layer (US 3097) with charcoal of maple, plum, boxwood, and deciduous oak, along with structural remains from the vault collapse (US 3096, 3069) and the internal wall framework (US 3007). A final, even smaller apsidal structure (UUSS 3037=3041), similarly oriented, occupies the southern portion of the cut.

(bibliography: De Santis et alii 2010, pp. 275-277)

contexts.name: Tomba 8 - vaso 7
contexts.description:
A miniaturized impasto vessel (no. 7) containing charred fragments of evergreen oak and boxwood comes from a large, deep oval well oriented north–south and cut into natural silt and clay. Midway down, the shaft narrowed to a smaller inner pit sealed by hefty blocks of lionato tuff and a quadrangular sandstone slab set horizontally at center. 

On the floor of this inner pit stood a ‘urna a capanna’ (hut-urn) encircled by eight miniaturized impasto vessels. The miniature bronzes comprised a spear with cast shaft placed in front of the urn’s doorway, while inside the urn two pairs of “double shields,” a pair of greaves, and a fibula were laid above the cremated bones, with a fragment of a bronze-sheet knife at the bottom. Abundant faunal remains of caprine and bovine were also preserved.

(bibliography: De Santis et alii 2011, p. 267)

contexts.name: Tomba 7
contexts.description:
The remains comes from two distint elements:

Vessel 1 — ‘boccale’ (jug): contained charcoal of evergreen oak.

Vessel 7 — ‘poppatoio’ (feeding bottle) with vertical ring handle: contained charcoal of evergreen oak and boxwood.

Small circular ‘pozzetto’, shallow and cut into natural silt and clay. The cover was almost entirely removed; the fill consisted of medium and small blocks of lionato tuff, with an additional travertine crust block to the west. On the floor sat the cinerary urn, closed with an inverted vessel base used as a lid; above it lay the miniaturized grave goods, including items typical of infant burials such as a ‘boccale’ and a ‘poppatoio’. One bowl contained sheep remains; lamb bones were also placed within the cinerary urn. Charred evergreen-oak fragments were found in vessels 1 and 7; boxwood was identified in vessel 7. Anthropology: sub-adult, c. 2 years; sex indeterminate.

Miniaturized impasto set comprising: a ‘boccale’ (1); a ‘scodella’ (2); a ‘piattello troncoconico’ used as the lid of the ‘poppatoio’ (3); a ‘tazzina’ (4; and another small cup, 6); a ‘scodellina carenata’ with horizontal grip (5); a ‘poppatoio’ with vertical ring handle (7); a vessel base reused as the cinerary lid (8); the cinerary urn (9); sheep ribs among the ashes (10).

(bibliography: De Santis et alii 2011, pp. 267-268)

contexts.name: Tomba 2 - olletta 6
contexts.description: Small, plain-surfaced ovoid olletta with a short flaring neck, from Tomb 2—a shallow, oval cremation pit cut into natural silt and clay and lined, covered, and filled with lionato tuff blocks and earth with traces of charcoal. The cinerary urn with roof lid stood upright at the center; the assemblage was entirely miniaturized. The olletta (no. 6) contained charred boxwood fragments; faunal offerings were placed nearby and in/over vessels 6, 8, and 10. Associated finds include nine impasto vessels concentrated to the west (lamp-tray, small jars—one net-decorated—a boat-shaped vessel, deep cup with over-rising handle, single-handled small bowl, three-footed plate, biconical olletta) and bronzes to the east (serpentine-arch fibula, Celano-type knife, paired “double shields” of sheet bronze with fastening hooks, and a spear). The deceased was a young adult male (c. 20–25 years). Calibrated 14C places the burial in the late Bronze–early Iron Age (ca. 11th–9th century BC).

contexts.name: deposito per derrate alimentari (US 1320)
contexts.description:
Seventh-century BC stratigraphic unit characterized by domestic/storage debris: several olle and hearth fittings, plus a small ‘dolio’ packed with charred broad-bean (Vicia faba) seeds—interpretable as a foodstuff deposit. Charcoal is abundant, dominated by evergreen oak (holm/cork oak), with lesser deciduous oak and a trace of boxwood.

(bibliography: de Santis et alii 2010, p. 279)

contexts.name: Dolium (US 285)
contexts.description:
A partially buried ‘dolio’ with four cylindrical lugs at its maximum girth cuts across the western sector, intersecting the perimeter drain and a hut posthole. It was subsequently scarred by the installation of a fire-related structure (US 3002), in use from the beginning of phase IIIB through the whole IV period, and later by historical works (Caesarian leveling and an early-medieval vine trench). The vessel was likely repurposed as a refuse container: inside were domestic materials—a lid, a cup fragment with an obliquely ribbed shoulder, fragments of hearth/stove fittings, containers for provisions, and a piece of bronze wire with triangular section. Environmental remains included charred caryopses of barley and einkorn (Triticum monococcum), charcoal of Prunus sp. and evergreen oak (holm/cork oak), and very fragmentary animal bones. Within the site sequence, the ‘dolio’ is attributed to phase IIIA, while a nearby infant tomb (Tomb 9) belongs to phases IIIB2/IVA1.

(bibliography: de Santis et alii 2010, pp. 273-274)

contexts.name: piano di concotto (US 1300)
contexts.description:
A fired-clay ‘piastra di cottura’ dating to the initial phase of Period III (phase IIIA, late 9th century BC) was identified near the southern edge of the excavation. Its surface was later truncated by several large 7th-century BC postholes. From the surrounding context came charred barley caryopses and charcoal of evergreen oak (holm/cork oak), indicating nearby firing and food-processing activities.

(bibliography: de Santis et alii 2010, p.274)

contexts.name: Pozzo - Area B (Caesar's Foro)
contexts.description:
Associated with the Period III–IV occupation in Area B, the well is roughly 0.8 m in diameter and more than 6 m deep. The upper stretch was unlined and equipped with footholds, while the lower shaft was strengthened with small blocks of lionato tuff where the natural deposits are most friable. It was dug through Paleotiber alluvium: clayey silts with pumice lenses near the top, grading into yellowish sands below; the water table lay about 6 m down (c. 8.40 m a.s.l.), and the shaft likely did not continue much beyond that level. 

On the floor were the only two complete (or fully reconstructable) vessels: a locally made globular jug in refined clay with painted bands and oblique motifs, and an imported kotyle datable to Early Protocorinthian (last quarter of the 8th century BC). Interpreted as a drinking set, they were probably placed intentionally when the well was first put into service. The overlying fills contained abundant refuse—table wares (cups, pyxides, red-impasto ollae), cooking pots and trays, storage containers (dolia, cylinder-ovoid ‘ollette’), hearth fittings and two spools—entirely fragmentary and redeposited, indicating dumping after the well fell out of use. The backfill appears to have been a single operation in the early 6th century BC, coinciding with site leveling and a new construction phase. Faunal remains include cattle, caprines, and pigs, as well as at least three juvenile dogs (under one year) bearing butchery and burning marks. Paleobotanical sampling recovered very abundant charred plant remains—grains of barley and wheat and broad-bean seeds—consistent with the contemporary habitation deposits.

(bibliography: de Santis et alii 2010, pp. 279-281)

contexts.name: Tomba 6 - undet. (Roma Foro di Cesare)
contexts.description:
A narrow, shallow rectangular pit with rounded corners, oriented northwest–southeast and cut into natural silt and clay, was found with its covering entirely removed; the fill consisted of the same sediment. The individual lay supine on the grave floor, head to the northwest, limbs extended, and was likely wrapped in a shroud fastened at the chest and feet. 

The assemblage was limited to personal ornaments: a necklace combining amber discoid beads, glass beads, conical amber buttons, amber pendants, and small gold spirals; multiple fibulae (including a serpentine-arch example with disc foot and several thickened-bow types, one large); a spiral wire hair-fastener; a small bronze wire ring with cylindrical pendants and amber beads; and loose bronze wire with amber fragments. Animal offerings—bovine and caprine remains—were placed near the right femur and behind the skull.

(bibliography: De Santis et alii 2011, p. 268)

contexts.name: Tomba 5 - dolio troncoconico
contexts.description:
A truncated-conical 'dolio' with a finger-impressed cordon below the rim was set at the bottom of a circular well cut into natural silt and clay; the shaft, filled and covered with blocks of lionato tuff, narrowed to a smaller pit sealed by a convex tuff block. Inside the 'dolio' stood the cinerary urn (a biconical olla with a horizontal handle and three conical bosses) closed by a conical lid, accompanied by six miniaturized impasto vessels (a three-footed plate/stool, a bowl, three plain 'ollette', and one 'olletta' with inturned rim). 

Miniature bronzes placed among the ashes inside the urn comprised a razor, a serpentine-arch fibula with spiral-disc foot, and a spear with cast shaft; a fragment of another serpentine-arch fibula came from the fill. Charred evergreen-oak wood (holm oak/cork oak) and pig remains were present in the fills. The interred individual was an adult male.

(bibliography: De Santis et alii 2011, p. 266)

contexts.name: Tomba 4 - undet. (Roma Foro di Cesare)
contexts.description:
A regular rectangular pit with rounded corners, oriented northwest–southeast and cut into natural silt and clay, contained an infant laid supine on the floor of the grave, head to the northwest, limbs extended, the left hand placed beneath the pelvis. The covering was missing; the fill—of the same sediment—yielded a few pottery fragments. The arrangement of skeletal parts observed during excavation suggests the body was wrapped in a binding or shroud. 

The grave goods, all of normal size, comprised two vessels at the feet and a third placed over the pelvis; two spindle whorls near the left femur; ornaments on the chest (small cast rings, an amber pendant, an amber discoid bead, a fibula with thickened bow and three suspension rings, and a necklace of amber discoid beads); a spiral wire hair-fastener beside the right side of the skull; and a cast bronze suspension ring at the feet. Faunal offerings (piglet remains) were set near the knees and the right foot, and charcoal of evergreen oak was present. On the basis of the assemblage, the burial is attributed to a female child aged approximately 4–5 years.

(bibliography: De Santis et alii 2011, p. 269)

contexts.name: Tomba 1 (Area funeraria dal Foro di Cesare)
contexts.description:
A shallow, oval cremation pit oriented east–west was uncovered, its cover and fill—small lionato tuff blocks mixed with earth—partly disturbed. The cinerary urn, laid horizontally with its lid placed beneath, occupied the eastern end, while the grave goods were arranged to the west. The assemblage, entirely miniaturized, comprised impasto pottery (including a biconical olla used as the urn with a roof-shaped lid, small net-decorated jars, a deep cup with a biforate handle, a single-handled bowl, a three-footed plate/stool, two askoi, a small jar with an inturned rim, and a boat-shaped vessel) and a few bronze items, notably “double shields” made from overlapping sheet discs with a central perforation and repoussé decoration, as well as a fragmentary serpentine-arch fibula. Faunal remains of young lambs were also present. Anthropological analysis indicates an adult male, about 30–40 years old. The burial belongs to the early Latial IIA1 horizon (roughly 11th–10th century BC), consistent with calibrated radiocarbon results spanning the later 13th to early 10th centuries BC.

(bibliography: De Santis et alii 2011, p. 264)

contexts.name: Carcer - Tullianum (sacred)
contexts.description:
The Carcer-Tullianum (the 'Mamertine Prison') was originally part of the Comitium in the Roman Forum, at the foot of the Capitoline Hill. The lower chamber, the Tullianum, contains a spring; recent investigations of the monument brought to light a votive deposit sealed under its floor.

Bibliography: Pagnoux, C., Celant, A., Coubray, S., Fiorentino, G., Zech-Matterne, V. 2013. The introduction of Citrus to Italy, with reference to the identification problems of seed remains. Vegetation History and Archaeobotany 22: 421–438. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00334-012-0389-4; Celant, A., Fiorentino, G. 2017. Macroremains of citrus fruit in Italy. In AGRUMED. Naples: Centre Jean Bérard.

contexts.name: small rectangular pit
contexts.description:
Small rectangular pit (c. 25 × 54 cm) found in 2010 close to the spring on the north-eastern side of the Tullianum, containing a votive deposit sealed under the floor of the Carcer-Tullianum and dated to the Augustan period (27 BC–AD 14). It yielded fifteen waterlogged seeds and a fragment of rind of Citrus, identified as citron (C. medica) and possibly lemon (C. cf. limon), among the earliest evidence for citrus in Rome.

Bibliography: Pagnoux, C., Celant, A., Coubray, S., Fiorentino, G., Zech-Matterne, V. 2013. The introduction of Citrus to Italy, with reference to the identification problems of seed remains. Vegetation History and Archaeobotany 22: 421–438. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00334-012-0389-4; Celant, A., Fiorentino, G. 2017. Macroremains of citrus fruit in Italy. In AGRUMED. Naples: Centre Jean Bérard.

contexts.name: Roma - Fori Imperiali - Templum Pacis (secred)
contexts.description:
The Templum Pacis (Forum of Peace) was built by Vespasian in AD 71–75 to celebrate the victory in the Jewish War, north-east of the Roman Forum. It was a large rectangular square surrounded on three sides by porticoes, with the temple of Pax at the back; the central area was laid out as a garden with planting beds and water features, as confirmed by the excavations carried out from 1998 by the Sovraintendenza Capitolina.

Bibliography: Celant, A. 2005. Le rose del Templum Pacis nell'antica Roma. Informatore Botanico Italiano 37: 898–899.

contexts.name: vasi
contexts.description:
Pots set in the planting beds of the garden of the Templum Pacis, dated to AD 71–75 (Vespasianic construction). Their contents were studied by A. Celant, who identified remains of roses cultivated in the garden of the complex.

Bibliography: Celant, A. 2005. Le rose del Templum Pacis nell'antica Roma. Informatore Botanico Italiano 37: 898–899.

contexts.name: Atrium Vestae - Well fills
contexts.description:
Fills of an Archaic well in the area of the Atrium Vestae, dated to the end of the 6th century BC. Context from the American Academy in Rome excavations of the area sacra of Vesta (1987–1996, R.T. Scott); charred plant remains studied by L. Costantini and J.A. Giorgi.

The charred plant remains. In Scott (ed.) 2009: 125–151; Costantini, L., Giorgi, J. 2001. Charred plant remains of the Archaic period from the Forum and Palatine. Journal of Roman Archaeology 14: 239–248.

contexts.name: Via Sacra - demolition debris
contexts.description:
Demolition debris along the Via Sacra, dated to the end of the 7th century BC. Context from the series of charred plant remains of the Archaic period from the Roman Forum and Palatine published by L. Costantini and J. Giorgi (2001), the first systematically sampled and floated assemblage from early Rome, which complemented the pioneering but unsystematic studies of H. Helbaek in the 1950s–1960s.

(eds), Storia dell'agricoltura italiana I: 221–233.

Construction deposit along the Via Sacra, dated to the end of the 6th century BC. Context from the series of charred plant remains of the Archaic period from the Roman Forum and Palatine published by L. Costantini and J. Giorgi (2001), the first systematically sampled and floated assemblage from early Rome, which complemented the pioneering but unsystematic studies of H. Helbaek in the 1950s–1960s.

contexts.name: Via Sacra - construction deposit - III-II BC

contexts.name: Pit III
contexts.description:
Sample from Pit III of the Sepolcreto Arcaico excavated by G. Boni, dated to the 8th–6th centuries BC. The 'Sepolcreto Arcaico' is the Iron Age cemetery discovered by Giacomo Boni at the beginning of the 20th century along the Via Sacra, next to the temple of Antoninus and Faustina in the Roman Forum. Van Kampen et al. (2005) re-examined Boni's manuscripts, maps, sections and stored materials to reconstruct the so-called 'IV strato' of 'pre-Republican age' – habitation layers with stone and perishable structures overlying and post-dating the burials – and presented the associated plant (A. Celant, M. Follieri) and animal remains (J. De Grossi Mazzorin, C. Minniti).

Bibliography: Van Kampen, I., Rathje, A., Celant, A., Follieri, M., De Grossi Mazzorin, J., Minniti, C. 2005. The pre-Republican habitation layers of the Via Sacra in Giacomo Boni's excavation of the Sepolcreto Arcaico. In Attema, P. et al. (eds), Papers in Italian Archaeology VI (BAR IS 1452). Oxford: 745–753.

contexts.name: Domus Tiberiana
contexts.description:
The Domus Tiberiana is the imperial palace on the north-western corner of the Palatine, facing the Roman Forum. Its first phase documented archaeologically is Neronian, built after the fire of AD 64; Domitian restored and enlarged it as an annex of his new palace, and under Hadrian its substructures were extended over the northern slope, covering the Republican Clivus Victoriae and reaching the Neronian Via Nova, along which ran a row of multi-storey tabernae. Excavations along the Via Nova and in the Domus were directed by M.A. Tomei (Soprintendenza) from the 1980s onwards.

Bibliography: Masi, A., Sadori, L., Carboni, F., Tomei, M.A. 2008. Contribution to the IV International Meeting of Anthracology; Carboni, F., Mosca, F., Puppo, P. 2014. La Domus Tiberiana sul Palatino: indagini recenti lungo la Via Nova. Rei Cretariae Romanae Fautorum Acta 43: 251ff.

contexts.sourceDating: second half of the 1st century AD
contexts.description:
SU 139, deposit beneath the floor of a taberna facing the Via Nova on the northern side of the Domus Tiberiana, dated to the second half of the 1st century AD (the Neronian–Flavian phases of the palace). Charcoal from this context was analysed by A. Masi and L. Sadori.

Bibliography: Masi, A., Sadori, L., Carboni, F., Tomei, M.A. 2008. Contribution to the IV International Meeting of Anthracology; Carboni, F., Mosca, F., Puppo, P. 2014. La Domus Tiberiana sul Palatino: indagini recenti lungo la Via Nova. Rei Cretariae Romanae Fautorum Acta 43: 251ff.

contexts.name: Palatino - NE Area
contexts.description:
North-eastern slope of the Palatine, facing the Colosseum valley and the Velia, investigated by Sapienza University of Rome under C. Panella from 2001 onwards. The excavations documented an Iron Age hut settlement along the present Via Sacra, an 8th-century BC sanctuary on the southern slope of the Velia, the sacred area identified with the Curiae Veteres and Archaic–Republican residential blocks and roads.

Bibliography: Ferrandes, A.F. 2024. Strade, santuari e domus tra Palatino e Velia nella media età repubblicana (IV–III secolo a.C.). 1. Stratigrafie, contesti, ricostruzioni (with texts by C. Armenio, E. Brienza, L. Fornaciari, A. Masi, D. Nonnis). Roma: Quasar; Armenio, C., Masi, A. 2024. In Ferrandes 2024: 501–506; Panella, C. et al. 2019. Curiae Veteres. contexts.description:
Votive pit documented in the Sapienza excavations directed by C. Panella on the north-eastern slopes of the Palatine (Panella 2011), whose charcoal was analysed by A. Celant (2011) within a study of wood use and palaeoenvironment.

Bibliography: Celant, A. 2011. Antracologia, utilizzazione del legno e ricostruzione paleoambientale. Origini 33: 237–248; Panella 2011 (as cited in the dataset).

contexts.name: Magna Mater (Cibele) Sanctuary
contexts.description:
The “Sanctuary of Magna Mater” is understood as a broader south-western Palatine area centred on the Temple of Magna Mater/Cybele, including the adjacent Temple of Victory, the Auguratorium (a small sacred building traditionally identified to the east of the temple terrace), the imperial-age balneum, and the service districts (circulation areas, drainage/sewers, working/storage spaces) that supported both ritual activity and the daily functioning of the complex. 

The temple itself was begun in 204 BC and dedicated in 191 BC, and its cult was closely connected to the Temple of Victory, which temporarily housed Cybele’s sacred stone before the Magna Mater temple was completed. 

The stratigraphic sequence highlighted by the 2006 study documents not only Roman phases (construction, monumentalisation, and later reorganisations), but also late-antique transformations: major reworkings in the 3rd–4th centuries AD, followed by progressive dismantling and abandonment (first clear abandonments c. 350–390 AD, then wider decline c. 420–450 AD), sporadic reuse as dump/overflow in the mid–late 5th century, and final collapse/definitive abandonment into the early 6th century.

contexts.name: Domus Tiberiana Southern Quarters
contexts.sourceDating: second half of the 4th - second half to end of the 5th century AD
contexts.description:
In the SW area south-west of the Domus Tiberiana, where service-facing rooms and sanitary/drainage installations played a major role. This area shows a clear imperial development: Domitianic rooms were reorganised in the Hadrianic phase into five vaulted spaces abutting the southern cryptoporticus, including a water container and a latrine, with further sewer-system refurbishments and at least one intervention around the turn of the 3rd–4th century (new branch and new hydraulic flooring).

A Trench cut in the area (Trench W), from wich the botanical samples derive, shows abandonment phases (c. 350–390 AD) affecting the broader complex, followed by a progressive retreat and use as dump in the Late Antiquity phase.

contexts.name: Aedes Victoriae - Temple of Victory (Trench V)
contexts.description:
The Temple of Victory on the south-western Palatine was dedicated in 294 BC by L. Postumius Megellus and stood immediately adjacent to the Temple of Magna Mater, with the small shrine of Victoria Virgo also in the same cluster. Ancient sources and later scholarship emphasise that the building remained an important landmark on the clivus Victoriae, and that it underwent substantial restoration in the late Republican/early Augustan period (perhaps connected with the Palatine fire of AD 3). In wider historical terms, the temple is also functionally intertwined with the Magna Mater sanctuary: traditions record that Cybele’s sacred stone was housed in the Temple of Victory between its arrival in Rome (204 BC) and the dedication of the Magna Mater temple (191 BC), reinforcing the idea of a tightly integrated sacred landscape.

Trench V—from which the botanical samples derive—is explicitly tied to foundation stratigraphy, and is therefore connected with the construction phase (and earliest monumental arrangement) of the Victory complex.

contexts.name: Service Quarter of Magna Mater Temple (Late Antiquity)
contexts.description: In the western area of the Magna Mater sanctuary stood a service area. The botanical samples derive from a trench (RZ) wich is a reference point for the late sequence of the area, because its deposits capture both restructuring and decline: after earlier imperial arrangements, the sector undergoes a 3rd–4th century AD reorganisation and then a pronounced trajectory of abandonment and secondary use.  Thrench RZ - and the overall area - is then explicitly linked to the mid–late 5th century pattern of sporadic reoccupation as dump/overflow ('inondazione'/'colmata'), before the final collapse dynamics that close the sequence into the early 6th century.

contexts.name: Trench R (outern sectorn of imperial balneum)
contexts.sourceDating: second half of the 4th - second half to end of the 5th century AD
contexts.description: Trench R is framed as part of the sector north of the imperial-age balneum, i.e., a transitional band between bath-related infrastructure and the broader sanctuary/service landscape and is linked with RZ as a key window onto the late antique life-history of the area: it participates in the same macro-processes of restructuring (3rd–4th centuries AD) and then progressive functional decline.

contexts.name: Roma - Colosseum (settlement)
contexts.description:
Begun under Vespasian (c. AD 70–72) and dedicated by Titus in AD 80 (with inaugural games), the Colosseum was completed and upgraded under the Flavians, including Domitian’s additions (from AD 82) and the development of the hypogeum. In Late Antiquity the monument remained in use but was increasingly shaped by repair cycles and changing entertainment practices: gladiatorial combat is conventionally considered to have ended in the early 5th century, while animal hunts (venationes) are still attested in AD 523. The building also underwent major restorations after 5th-century earthquake damage (e.g., the well-known restoration associated with Rufius Caecina Felix Lampadius after AD 443). 

A key infrastructural component throughout its life was its complex drainage system, including major East and West sewer collectors, which later preserved sealed Late Antique deposits.

contexts.name: West sewer of the Colosseum
contexts.sourceDating: second half of the 4th century AD
contexts.description: The West collector belongs to the Colosseum’s drainage network and slopes gradually outward. Investigations begun in 1973 found clear evidence that the conduit became blocked and inactive in the second half of the 4th century AD, preserving a sealed deposit of waste flushed from within the amphitheatre. This waterterlogged sediment trapped a rich assemblage of plant remains (seeds, fruits, leaves) and even a small set of worked wooden objects; the botanical spectrum is consistent with food debris from spectators alongside incidental plant inputs.

contexts.name: East sewer of the Colosseum
contexts.sourceDating: second half of the 4th century AD
contexts.description:
The East collector was explored during restoration/strengthening works on the amphitheatre foundations, in a broader context where sections of the sewer system had been sealed for roughly 1,600 years. Its sediment is described as largely sandy, with organic plant matter preserved under asphyctic/reducing, waterlogged conditions, allowing recovery (via water-separation) of an unusually “fresh-looking” assemblage. 

The recorded taxa include a wide range of cultivated foods (e.g., vine, fig, olive, nuts, cereals), spices/oil plants, and also ornamental and wild/ruderal species—a combination interpreted as reflecting both consumption inside the amphitheatre and the local vegetation history of the monument’s sealed micro-environment.

contexts.name: Colosseum Valley
contexts.description:
The Colosseum valley, between the Palatine, Velia, Oppian and Caelian, was originally a natural valley crossed by a stream, with prehistoric, protohistoric and Early Iron Age frequentation. It became progressively structured from the Orientalising and Archaic periods (roads, sewers, the Curiae Veteres sanctuary), was reorganised under Augustus, absorbed into Nero's Domus Aurea after AD 64 and then transformed by the Flavians with the Colosseum and the Meta Sudans fountain. The excavations of Sapienza University of Rome in the Meta Sudans sector (1986–2003) and related coring documented the deep stratigraphy of the valley.

Bibliography: Celant, A., Magri, D. 1999. Archaeobotanical study of a sediment core from the Colosseum valley. Riassunti 94° Congresso della Società Botanica Italiana (Ferrara): 40.

contexts.name: Sediment core in the Colosseum Valley
contexts.description:
Sediment core drilled in the Colosseum valley and studied by A. Celant and D. Magri (1999) for its archaeobotanical content, providing a record of the valley-floor deposits beneath the monumental phases of the area.

Bibliography: Celant, A., Magri, D. 1999. Archaeobotanical study of a sediment core from the Colosseum valley. Riassunti 94° Congresso della Società Botanica Italiana (Ferrara): 40.

contexts.name: Arch of Constantine and Meta Sudans Area
contexts.description:
The Area between the Colosseum, the Velia, the Palatine and the Caelian is a long-lived urban palimpsest. Before monumental Rome, it was a natural valley crossed by the 'Rivo Labicano', with evidence of prehistoric/protohistoric and Early Iron Age activity and the gradual installation of tracks, drainage works and early infrastructures along the watercourse and the valley-floor routes.

From the Orientalising and Archaic periods onward, the area becomes increasingly structured, including an early sacred focus on the north-eastern Palatine slopes—often discussed in relation to the Curiae Veteres tradition—while roads and sewers are repeatedly rebuilt through the Republican centuries. In the Augustan reorganisation, the road network and adjacent blocks were substantially renewed; within this framework an earlier, smaller “Meta Sudans” complex (with a compital shrine) preceded the later Flavian fountain.

After the fire of AD 64 the valley was heavily remodelled and absorbed into the Neronian Domus Aurea landscape; the Flavians later replaced key Neronian features with the Colosseum and its surrounding urban piazza, including the large monumental Meta Sudans at a major crossroads. The Constantinian phase fixed the best-known image of the area: the Arch of Constantine—dedicated in AD 315 on the triumphal route—reframed the space in front of the amphitheatre.

In Late Antiquity, the Meta Sudans remained in use into the 5th century, before progressive infilling and the obstruction of drainage channels contributed to its decline. Modern transformations culminated in the demolition of the standing remains in the 1930s, during fascist re-planning of the road system. 

Archaeological work has been pivotal for reconstructing this long sequence: a large-scale stratigraphic excavation in the Meta Sudans sector ran from 1986 to 2003 (with major phases through the 1990s and early 2000s), documenting the valley’s deep stratigraphy and identifying substantial Augustan/Claudian structures beneath the Flavian fountain. The same research framework also connected with targeted investigations around the Arch of Constantine’s foundations during restoration campaigns.

contexts.name: Medieval dump
contexts.description:
Stratigraphic tests carried out along the southern and eastern sides of the Arch of Constantine (notably in the context of restoration-related investigations) show that post-classical deposits are extremely discontinuous in this sector, largely because modern clearances and restorations lowered ground levels and removed much of the later stratigraphy. Within this heavily truncated sequence, one of the few clear post-Roman features is the bottom of a well/shaft on the eastern side of the Arch, interpreted as a domestic refuse deposit (“butto”) containing abundant animal bone and a ceramic assemblage dated no later than the 14th century; the feature is plausibly connected with a small house documented in early-modern (16th-century) views of the area.

Within this heavily truncated sequence, one of the few clear post-Roman features is the bottom of a well/shaft on the eastern side of the Arch, interpreted as a domestic refuse deposit (“butto”) containing abundant animal bone and a ceramic assemblage dated no later than the 14th century; the feature is plausibly connected with a small house documented in early-modern (16th-century) views of the area. 

The same investigations also note later intrusive/maintenance works in the sector—such as a large pit dated to the early 17th century and drainage channels associated with post-medieval restoration activity—highlighting how repeated interventions reshaped the immediate surroundings of the monument from the early modern period onward.

contexts.name: Early Modern disposal Pit
contexts.description:
The “discard pit” is located at the bottom of a stairwell inside the façade-tower of the complex rebuilt under Leo IV (847–855). In the 15th century, restoration works attributed to Cardinal Carrillo (1424–1434) included the closure of a ground-floor door, which effectively turned the lower part of the staircase into a convenient dumping space. The filling activity is dated —mainly by ceramics— to the late 15th century, while the final sealing/closure is placed around the mid-16th century, possibly linked to the establishment of the Augustinian community (1564). 


Archaeologically, the pit is composed of two main layers: US 3 and US 4. The entire fill is dominated by hay, within which ca. 6,000 desiccated (mummified) plant macroremains (35 taxa) were recovered, together with abundant food refuse and faunal remains. The assemblage is consistent with table/kitchen waste (cereals, pulses, fruits, vegetables/spices; plus shells, fish, birds, mammals), rather than a latrine-type deposit.

contexts.name: Ambiente 3
contexts.description:
During the 2011–2012 an excavation campaign was carried out within a former early-17th-century arched porch/portico, later subdivided into three rooms: Ambienti 1–3, belonging to the monastic complex. The work followed earlier investigations in the cloister/garden area and aimed to clarify the stratigraphic sequence in this service-facing part of the monument. 

Within Ambiente 3, an Imperial-period brick wall oriented NE/SW testifies the use of the area in the Roman period. The area appears to have remained open in the early Middle Ages, with beaten-earth surfaces, including one made with reused basalt paving stones (basoli) that is possibly connected to the Leo IV basilica phase.
Later, deposits and installations suggest a later medieval building-yard—likely associated with the 13th-century cloister works, before the area was finally reconfigured by the 17th-century portico. A key deposit from Ambiente 3, US 555 (charred timbers, many iron nails, tile fragments), has been interpreted as an accumulation of burnt roof-wood gathered on-site.

contexts.name: "Nuovo Mercato di Testaccio"'s Archeological Area
contexts.description:
The archaeological area beneath the Nuovo Mercato di Testaccio lies in the sub-Aventine plain, immediately north of Monte Testaccio and close to the ancient river port (Emporium) on the left bank of the Tiber. From the late 3rd–2nd century BC onward, this waterfront district was progressively equipped with major commercial infrastructure, including large warehouse complexes such as the Porticus Aemilia and other horrea, while Monte Testaccio itself formed (1st–3rd century AD) as a controlled mound of discarded transport amphorae linked to large-scale provisioning. 

Archaeological investigations carried out during 2005-2009 investigated roughly one hectare area, exposing a sequence wich starts in early-imperial phase (Augustan–Flavian horizon). In this phase the area is occupied by open enclosures/courtyards and service routes, small rectangular rooms at their margins, and structures built using stacked, reused empty amphorae. The area is therefore interpreted as part of a large managed area for the disposal and reuse of building/transport containers, with adjacent spaces plausibly functioning as storage with beaten-earth floors. 
A subsequent mid-imperial phase (Trajanic–Hadrianic) is represented by construction levels of a trapezoidal horreum: rows of rectangular rooms arranged around (or facing) a broad central space described as porticoed, although only the foundation/building levels are preserved. 

Later medieval traces are slight and discontinuous, while post-medieval layers document the area’s longer-term shift toward rural/agricultural use before modern urbanisation.

Bibliography: D’Alessandro, Lucilla, “Il quadro territoriale. La piana del Testaccio nell’antichità: sviluppo storico e dinamiche insediative”, in : D’Alessandro, Lucilla, Anfore adriatiche a Roma: I dati del Nuovo Mercato Testaccio, Pessac, Ausonius éditions, collection PrimaLun@ 24, 2025, 53-86, https://una-editions.fr/lo-scavo-del-nuovo-mercato-testaccio-roma [consulté le 22/03/2025].

contexts.name: samples from production contexts
contexts.description:
Samples from production contexts of the excavations beneath the Nuovo Mercato di Testaccio (2005–2009), in the sub-Aventine plain near the ancient river port. Their analysis (Stellati et al. 2013) provided new data on land use and crop production within the urban area of Rome.

Bibliography: Stellati, A., Colaianni, G., Fiorentino, G., Sebastiani, R., Contino, A. 2013. Land use and crop production in the urban area of Rome: new data from the 'Nuovo Mercato' of Monte Testaccio (Rome, Italy). 16th Conference of the IWGP, Abstract Book: 158–159.

The context location is plotted arbitrarily at the centre of the broader reference site, as the specific sampling spot cannot be reconstructed with greater fidelity.

For a full description of the archaeological context, see the site's card.

contexts.name: Roma - Centocelle - Villa delle Terme (funerary)
contexts.description:
The Centocelle archaeological park, on the south-eastern outskirts of Rome along the Via Casilina, occupies the area of the former 'Francesco Baracca' airfield. Preventive investigations by the Sovraintendenza Capitolina in the 1990s, within the planned Sistema Direzionale Orientale (SDO), documented frequentation since prehistory and three Roman villas: the villa 'ad duas lauros', the 'Villa della Piscina' and the 'Villa delle Terme'. The 'Villa delle Terme' owes its name to its bath suite, the only part of the original complex that survived the destruction caused by modern pozzolana quarries; a burial (Tomb 1) in trench T.507 was sampled for plant remains.

Bibliography: Gioia, P., Volpe, R. (eds) 2004. Centocelle I. Roma S.D.O. Le indagini archeologiche. Soveria Mannelli: Rubbettino; Volpe, R. (ed.) 2007. Centocelle II. Roma S.D.O. Le indagini archeologiche. Soveria Mannelli: Rubbettino.
