contexts.site: Roma - Centocelle - Villa ad duas lauros
contexts.description:
The Centocelle archaeological park, on the south-eastern outskirts of Rome along the Via Casilina, occupies the area of the former 'Francesco Baracca' airfield. Preventive investigations by the Sovraintendenza Capitolina in the 1990s, within the planned Sistema Direzionale Orientale (SDO), documented frequentation since prehistory and three Roman villas: the villa 'ad duas lauros', the 'Villa della Piscina' and the 'Villa delle Terme'. contexts.description:

contexts.name: Fiumicino - Lingua d'Oca lacustrine sediments
contexts.description:
The Lingua d’Oca–Interporto (LOI) sequence comes from lacustrine/wetland sediments sampled in 2001 near the Lingua d’Oca canal (c. 2 m a.s.l.), during an archaeological survey carried out in the area of Fiumicino International Airport, in a sector formerly occupied by the Stagno di Maccarese wetland. The uppermost c. 170 cm—made up of reclaimed deposits and agricultural soil—were intentionally excluded from palaeobotanical sampling, while the underlying sequence was sampled systematically (64 samples at 5-cm intervals along c. 320 cm). 

Tiber delta, where lake-level shifts, episodes of marine-water intrusion, flood events, eutrophication and phases of desiccation repeatedly reshaped local environments and vegetation cover. Within this long-term instability, the palaeobotanical signal also documents human presence through micro-charcoal trends and “anthropogenic markers” (notably cereal-type pollen and other cultivation indicators), which become more visible in the later Holocene. In the Roman period, the published synthesis explicitly links the LOI evidence to “exploitation” of the area, including a chenopod-dominated marshland interpreted as compatible with saltwork environments, alongside woodland components dominated by evergreen and deciduous oaks.

Bibliography: Di Rita, Celant & Magri, Holocene environmental instability…, Journal of Paleolimnology 44 (2010), 51–67.

contexts.name: Oak sample URLS F15
contexts.description:
URLS F15 is a deciduous oak (Quercus) specimen from Lingua d’Oca (Fiumicino), described as a wooden pile embedded in a light-grey clay layer in the coastal area west of Rome near the Tiber delta; the context is noted as marshy until modern reclamation (1925), with traces of Roman-age drainage also reported. 

The specimen is singled out as the oldest successfully genotyped oak examined in Deguilloux et alii 2006 and yielded a chloroplast haplotype (“a”) that was then identified in nearby modern oak populations, supporting the interpretation that the timber used at Lingua d’Oca was locally sourced.

contexts.name: Roma - Osteria del Curato - Via Cinquefrondi (settlement)
contexts.site: Roma - Osteria del Curato - Via Cinquefrondi
contexts.description:
Osteria del Curato–Via Cinquefrondi is a multi-phase Copper Age settlement in south-eastern Rome (Tuscolana corridor, close to the GRA), set along the left bank of the Fosso di Gregna. The site was first recognised in 1972 in foundation trenches within an already urbanised zone, and was later investigated through preventive excavations in 2004–2005, split into multiple separate work areas (A–D) because of modern buildings and property boundaries. The excavated surface alone extends for over 2 hectares, while the overall settlement is thought to have reached c. 4.5 hectares along the palaeo-channel margin.

Archaeologically, two main occupation horizons are recognised, partly superimposed: an earlier Laterza phase (Late Copper Age) extending toward the stream/NE, and a later Ortucchio phase (Final Copper Age) shifting to the SW. Within these horizons, excavators documented hut-related layouts (posthole patterns and curvilinear foundation slots), pits/pozzetti, small channels, areas of burning/“concotto”, and—especially in wetter sectors—stone/cobble spreads and compacted surfaces interpreted as working or drained outdoor areas. A funerary component is also present (inhumations and chamber-like graves), and some parts of the settlement show complex internal organisation (e.g., bounded areas defined by channels).

Finally, the site is a key reference for Copper Age subsistence in the Roman hinterland because it yielded exceptionally rich archaeobotanical contexts, sampled from three features in different sectors: a cereal-storage facility (US 2358/2359), a hearth/processing deposit (US 2362), and a deep combustion feature/oven (US 215). These produced very large charred assemblages dominated by hulled barley, emmer, einkorn, and—in the oven—fava bean, providing direct evidence for cultivation, crop processing and storage practices within the Ortucchio horizon.

Bibliography (core): Anzidei et al. 2007 (Atti XL Riunione Scientifica IIPP); Carboni & Anzidei 2013; Anzidei & Carboni (eds.) 2020

contexts.name: Cereal storage pit (Silo) – US 2358 (cut) / US 2359 (fill)
contexts.site: Roma - Osteria del Curato - Via Cinquefrondi
contexts.description:
In the western part of the excavation (Sector G), a small cereal storage feature was identified and interpreted as a silo: US 2358 (structure/cut) and US 2359 (fill). The preserved portion measures roughly 0.85 × 0.80 × 0.20 m and was cut into a grey-reddish pozzolana/tuff unit (“Villa Senni”). Although truncated at the top, the internal morphology (a depressed end, slightly curving sides, and what was interpreted as a short “slide” and an arched/curved element suggesting an entrance) led excavators to propose it belonged to a more complex, partly subterranean, “pouch-shaped” facility rather than a simple open pit. The fill yielded tens of thousands of carbonised cereal grains, dominated by hulled barley (Hordeum vulgare), emmer (Triticum dicoccum) and einkorn (Triticum monococcum), together with arable weeds—clear evidence for bulk storage and/or the burning of stored crops.

Bibliography: Anzidei et al. 2007a; Anzidei & Carboni (eds.) 2020. .

contexts.name: Hearth / processing deposit – US 2362
contexts.site: Roma - Osteria del Curato - Via Cinquefrondi
contexts.description:
US 2362 is a shallow, oval combustion-related feature (c. 1.70 × 1.10 m, depth c. 0.05 m) recorded in Sector A and attributed to Ortucchio Phase III. The context is archaeobotanically exceptional: flotation recovered 14,697 cereal grains, with a crop spectrum dominated by einkorn and emmer, accompanied by hulled barley and minor components, plus small quantities of legumes and arable weeds. The concentration and composition were interpreted less as “ordinary hearth sweepings” and more as evidence for cereal-processing episodes (e.g., cleaning/dehusking and possibly parching/toasting prior to storage or consumption), with the hearth acting as the locus where processing by-products accumulated and were carbonised.

Bibliography: Anzidei et al. 2007a; Anzidei & Carboni (eds.) 2020. .

contexts.name: Deep combustion feature / oven – US 215
contexts.site: Roma - Osteria del Curato - Via Cinquefrondi
contexts.sourceDating: 2500 - 2330 a.C. cal 1s (3935 ± 60 BP) - facies di Ortucchio
contexts.description:
US 215 (Sector D) is a large, deep, pit-like combustion installation (reported as c. 1.60 m wide and up to 1.20 m deep), with walls showing intense firing/reddening and a fill rich in charcoal and burned material. A key archaeobotanical signal is the recovery of numerous fava bean (Vicia faba) cotyledons; one cotyledon provided a radiocarbon date (LTL990A: 3935±60 BP, calibrated to the mid–late 3rd millennium BC), anchoring the context within Ortucchio Phase III. The combination of structure form and botanical content supports interpretation as a specialised feature linked to heating/processing activities (potentially including food processing), rather than a simple domestic fire spot.

Bibliography: Anzidei et al. 2007a; Anzidei & Carboni (eds.) 2020. .

contexts.name: Imperial 'Portus' of Fiumicino
contexts.description:
The Port of Trajan was designed to reuse the lighthouse and quays of the Port of Claudius, which became the outer basin of the new harbor system. To these structures Trajan added a hexagonal basin covering 33 hectares, a monumental work of engineering that multiplied the docking points for ships. The emperor also had several canals dug, including the Fossa Traiana — the modern Fiumicino canal. These waterways allowed floodwaters to discharge into the sea, freeing Rome from the scourge of inundations.

In the 2nd and 3rd centuries, the growing importance of the harbor led to the development of a permanent settlement, which in 314 CE officially became a city under the name Portus Romae. Made independent from Ostia and enclosed by powerful walls, the settlement continued for several centuries to receive attention from central authorities, who were keen to keep the capital’s supply system efficient.

As the coastline advanced and the landscape changed, the Portus area gradually turned into marshland. Between the Middle Ages and the modern era, this process led to the near-total silting up of the harbor basin. The inhabited center, however, survived.

Source: MOSI record ID F94E21004510001-3_Sito-1, author Marrucci Maddalena (content manager: Marrucci Maddalena), compiled in 2024, https://gna.cultura.gov.it (original in Italian; personal translation).

contexts.name: Tansversal Canal (Canale Trasverso)
contexts.description:
Canale Trasverso was an engineered transverse channel that connected parts of the harbour system with the river-side waterways (under strong river influence). 

Stratigraphically, it includes deltaic sands at depth and a long canal-filling sequence with silts/clays containing pottery, wood fragments and molluscs—consistent with repeated dredging and reworking within an active harbour–canal environment. 

Archaeobotanical evidence (plant macroremains) is richer than in PTS13: 10 depth-interval samples between ~8.60 and 4.60 m contained enough seeds/fruits for study. Non-seed macroremains include frequent Posidonia oceanica fibres and scattered wood/bark fragments (e.g., Pinus cf. sylvestris, Ulmus, Alnus, Quercus sect. suber), again consistent with mixed marine debris and fluvial transport and harbour-canal maintenance dynamics. 

Overall, PTS5 captures a canal environment where plant input reflects both local wetland vegetation and anthropic disturbance/consumption waste, with changing salinity/river influence documented by the integrated proxy studies. 

Bibliography: Salomon et al. 2012; Sadori et al. 2010; Mazzini et al. 2011; Pepe et al. 2013; Giardini et al. 2013.

contexts.name: Dock (Darsena) area (PTS13)
contexts.description:
PTS13 is a sediment core taken inside the Portus archaeological area, in the inner docking zone (the darsena/dock linked to the Claudian basin and later integrated within the wider Claudian–Trajanic harbour system). The core records the transition from pre-harbour deltaic deposits to harbour infilling sediments, with a long sequence of silty clays that accumulated during the functioning and progressive silting-up of the dock area. 
Archaeobotanical evidence (plant macroremains) is sparse but informative: only 6 depth-interval samples between ~4.90 and 1.70 m yielded enough seeds/fruits for analysis, and a major timber horizon occurs between 3.60 and 2.90 m. 
The remains are consistent with a dock setting repeatedly receiving floating plant debris from both marine/coastal environments (Posidonia) and the fluvial–wetland mosaic around the Tiber delta, with periodic phases of quieter vs more energetic (flood-influenced) conditions also suggested by the associated microfaunal proxies. 

Bibliography: Sadori et al. 2010; Mazzini et al. 2011; Pepe et al. 2013; Giardini et al. 2013.

contexts.name: Terme dei Cisiari
contexts.description:
The "Terme dei Cisiari" stand in Regio II, Insula II, near the Porta Romana and the Decumanus. Built in the first half of the 2nd century AD (Hadrianic phase) and remodelled in the 3rd century, the complex is best known for the frigidarium mosaic depicting two concentric “city walls” and small two-wheeled carriages (cisia), which gave the building its modern name and has been linked—though not conclusively—to a professional guild of carriage drivers. Recent archaeological work has also shown that the imperial bath-building was conditioned by earlier, Late-Republican structures in the same insula, whose walls and layout were partly re-used and adapted during later phases. A key infrastructural element for the bath’s operation was a groundwater-lifting installation in the southern service sector: a wooden waterwheel/noria system, discovered in the 1990s, that supplied water for the bathing facilities and is crucial for understanding how small/medium bath complexes in Ostia could exploit the water table.

M. Bedello Tata & S. Fogagnolo, “Una ruota idraulica da Ostia,” in Aquam in altum exprimere (Ausonius).

contexts.name: "Vano della ruota”(waterwheel room) and associated finds
contexts.sourceDating: end 1st century AD - beginning 2nd century AD
contexts.description:
A wooden wheel was installed in a long, narrow service room in the southern part of the baths, an area repeatedly modified into Late Imperial times. Excavation showed that this “wheel room” re-used earlier masonry (including Late-Republican walls later refaced and heightened) and reached more than 3 m below the modern walking level, revealing deep features interpreted as groundwater-drainage works and even traces of a timber-lined rectangular structure plausibly connected with a well or earlier water-collection arrangement. The installation is interpreted as a water-lifting device drawing directly on the water table; in popular reconstructions for this building, the wheel could be powered by human traction (treadwheel), raising water toward an upper reservoir feeding the bath complex.

From the same stratigraphic context came wooden macro-remains connected both to the device itself and to other objects recovered together (tools, pins, and a small female statuette). The identified taxa are overwhelmingly deciduous oak (29 pieces) and, more rarely, silver fir (4 pieces), suggesting the deliberate selection of robust timbers for structural/mechanical components and associated artefacts.

Bibliography: M. Bedello Tata & S. Fogagnolo, 2005

contexts.name: Lago Albano - Villaggio delle Macine (underwater)
contexts.description:
'Villaggio delle Macine' is a pile-dwelling (wooden-platform) lakeshore settlement on Lake Albano, south of Rome. The site is exceptional both in scale (about 1–2 ha) and in the richness of its archaeological and environmental evidence, helped by favourable waterlogged preservation in parts of the deposit. It was already known from mid-20th-century observations and underwater recoveries, but systematic excavations began in 2001 and expanded as lake-level fluctuations progressively exposed larger portions of the palisaded/platform area. Current evidence indicates a long-lived occupation spanning the end of the Early Bronze Age and developing mainly during the early Middle Bronze Age; radiocarbon dates on wooden elements place the settlement broadly within the 2nd millennium BC (reported as 2140–1490 cal BC, 2σ, on 7 samples).

Bibliography: Angle et al.(2014); Angle et al. (2019); Achino et al. (2021).

contexts.name: undet. (Lago Albano - Villaggio delle Macine)
contexts.description:
Generic sampling unit for the plant macroremains of the pile-dwelling 'Villaggio delle Macine' on Lake Albano (Castel Gandolfo), analysed by M. Carra, L. Cattani and M. Rizzi in their study of the subsistence economy of the Early–Middle Bronze Age settlement.

Bibliography: Carra, M., Cattani, L., Rizzi, M. 2007. L'economia di sussistenza al Villaggio delle Macine (Castel Gandolfo, Roma) su basi paleocarpologiche. Atti XL Riunione Scientifica IIPP: 775–786.

contexts.name: Allumiere - La Fontanaccia (settlement)
contexts.description:
The site yielded the remains of a substantial terraced villa from the Roman period, probably abandoned in the early 2nd century AD. All the archaeobotanical remains come from a modest rural house built among the villa’s rubble and dating to the 5th century AD. 
It is unfortunately impossible to determine the precise location of the individual contexts ‘Because [...] the archaeobotanical material, all preserved by charring, was recovered from the hut floor without using a grid system.

contexts.description: From the floor of this modest Late Antique ‘hut’, a large amount of charred material was recovered. The archaeobotanical samples were divided into 12 units, but the lack of further reference points makes it impossible to provide a distinct attribution for each of them

contexts.name: Mura di S. Stefano
contexts.site: Anguillara Sabazia - Mura de Santo Stefano
contexts.description:
The "Mura di Santo Stefano" site is a prominent rural complex set along a diverticulum of the Via Clodia, on the southern side of Lake Bracciano. Archaeology indicates an initial 1st-century AD rural phase, followed by the construction (late 2nd century AD) of an imposing brick-faced, three-storey main building—a landmark structure whose appearance is also documented in early modern antiquarian drawings (Ligorio; later Piranesi). The standing remains preserve the logic of a multi-level architectural design (with internal divisions and a nearby cistern/water installation), framing the site as a high-status villa complex (“villa-praetorium”) within the broader imperial countryside of southern Etruria. Later phases include progressive decline and reuse, with the overall abandonment of the complex ultimately placed by recent research around the 16th century, and a final, purely funerary episode in 1856–87 during a malaria outbreak, when the area was used as a burial ground.

During the early medieval phase (9th–11th centuries AD) - the key horizon for the archaeobotanical evidence - the Roman complex was reoccupied and transformed, including the creation of a church dedicated to Santo Stefano (the surviving apse is on the NE side in the GNA description), and the area seems to have hosted a small-scale settlement/burial focus around the reused Roman structures. 

Bibliography: Costantini, Napolitano & Whitehouse 1983; Van de Noort & Whitehouse 2009; GNA record, MOSI J54E21003590001, Sito 447, Author: Marrucci Maddalena.

contexts.name: ditch of the main building
contexts.site: Anguillara Sabazia - Mura de Santo Stefano
contexts.description:
A ditch-like feature encircling the Main Building and from a well/cistern in the vestibule. 

During the British School at Rome excavations, west, north and south trenches were cut across this shallow circuit-ditch; carbonised plant remains (c. 350 g of seeds) were recovered from the latter two of these trenches, using by dry- and wet-sieving on contexts [345], [374], [379] and [450]. Associated pottery (including sparse glaze and vetrina) points to deposition in the 10th–11th centuries, and the excavators interpret the deposit as stored crops (for consumption and/or sowing) disrupted by a fire and subsequently scattered. The published identifications highlight a cereal-and-pulse package typical of early medieval agrarian storage: free-threshing wheat, barley, emmer/spelt-type wheats, and a substantial legume component dominated by broad beans, with minor pulses and arable weeds also present.

contexts.name: S. Angelo Romano - Grotta dello Sventatoio (settlement)
contexts.site: S. Angelo Romano - Grotta dello Sventatoio
contexts.description:
In 1984, a group of speleoligsts from the Rome section of the Italian Alpine Club (C.A.I.) discovered and reported the presence of ceramic fragments in chambers B, C, D, and E of Grotta dello Sventatoio. A subsequent inspection made it possible to systematically collect all the material found on the surface, leading to the identification of about 8,000 coarse-ware ceramic sherds, belonging to at least 400 vessels. In addition to the pottery, a number of bronze objects, bone and stone artefacts, faunal remains, and some human bones of infants were recovered. Several vessels, found almost intact, contained seeds of wheat, barley, and broad beans. The finds indicate that the cave, used as a cult place, was frequented throughout the entire Middle Bronze Age.

(description from: https://sabinasacra.lad-sapienza.it/monumento/?tb=luogo_di_interesse&id=434 ; author: L. Alessandri; personal translation)

contexts.name: Room D
contexts.site: S. Angelo Romano - Grotta dello Sventatoio
contexts.sourceDating: fase avanzata della media età del Bronzo
contexts.description:
Room (chamber) D of the Grotta dello Sventatoio (Sant'Angelo Romano), one of the chambers where cavers of the CAI Rome section reported pottery in 1984 and from which about 8,000 sherds of at least 400 vessels were collected; several almost intact vessels contained seeds of wheat, barley and broad bean. The cave was used as a cult place throughout the Middle Bronze Age; the sampled material belongs to an advanced phase of the period.

Bibliography: Costantini, L., Costantini Biasini, L. 2007. Economia agricola del Lazio a sud del Tevere tra Bronzo antico e Bronzo medio. Atti XL Riunione Scientifica IIPP: 787–801; Sabina Sacra (LAD Sapienza), scheda Grotta dello Sventatoio (L. Alessandri).

contexts.name: Piano di Comunità (Veio)
contexts.description:
Piano (or Quarto) di Comunità is a long ridge projecting south/south-east from the main Veii plateau, traversed by a major urban route and strategically overlooking the Cremera valley toward the Tiber. Its archaeological record is multi-period: occupation begins in the 9th century BC with scattered hut nuclei; from the late 7th century BC the district develops as a craft quarter with specialised workshops (notably for tableware and 'bucchero' production). In the 6th century BC the area undergoes significant urban and infrastructural works: terracing walls, road arrangements, and a dense hydraulic system (cuniculi, a monumental cistern, and wells). Architectural terracottas and votive material suggest one or more public/sacred buildings active between the later 6th and 5th centuries BC, supporting the long-standing hypothesis that the summit ridge may relate to an “historic acropolis” and the sphere of the city’s major cults. 

From the late Republican period, the visible remains on the summit are dominated by a large terraced villa/domus complex (cd. “Edificio Lanciani”), organised on multiple levels. The residential core is arranged around a cruciform atrium with an impluvium; service/storage spaces occupy the north-eastern sector, where a rectangular cistern is also reported, while a monumental circular cistern (c. 10 m diameter) belongs to the broader water-management system of the complex. The villa is described as abandoned by Late Antiquity / the 5th century AD in synthesis accounts, while the summit area also preserves traces of later reorganisation and spoliation processes. 


Bibliography: AA.VV., Il contributo degli scavi di Piano di Comunità alla conoscenza dell’abitato di Veio: materiali dal riempimento di un pozzo sul pianoro sommitale, in G. Bartoloni (ed.), L’abitato etrusco di Veio… I. Cisterne, pozzi e fosse (2009). ; B. Belelli Marchesini, “Piano di Comunità – complesso archeologico”, in Guida Archeologica del Parco di Veio (2021).

contexts.name: well from Room A of the Domus
contexts.description:
The archaeobotanical assemblage comes from the intentional backfilling/obliteration of a well intercepted below the domus, in the S/W corner (within “Ambiente A”). The fill is described as a unitary operation, articulated into two main dumping episodes separated by deliberate levelling/sealing actions (including layers of roof-tiles), with a strongly ceremonial character inferred for the uppermost phase; overall, the deposit contains an exceptionally large amount of material (tens of thousands of fragments), dominated by tableware (especially bucchero), alongside faunal remains and other classes. Chronologically, the assemblage as a whole is treated as a major sample of Veii’s 6th–5th century BC material culture, while elements from the deepest part help frame the obliteration as occurring after the Roman takeover, in a mid-Republican horizon. 

The macro-remains include carbonised plant material and worked/charred wood, interpreted as either accidental input from local vegetation or deliberate deposition with symbolic/votive value, also in light of associated carpological and faunal evidence. Palynological comparisons support a reconstruction of a landscape composed of mixed deciduous woodland with evergreen sub-Mediterranean elements, and cereal cultivation (notably wheat and barley) at regional scale. 

Bibliography: AA.VV., Il contributo degli scavi di Piano di Comunità alla conoscenza dell’abitato di Veio: materiali dal riempimento di un pozzo sul pianoro sommitale, in G. Bartoloni (ed.), L’abitato etrusco di Veio… I. Cisterne, pozzi e fosse (2009).

contexts.name: Castle of S. Severa
contexts.description:
The Castello di Santa Severa occupies a strategic stretch of coast north of Rome, where the Etruscan port-settlement of Pyrgi (connected to Caere/Cerveteri) developed from the 7th century BC onward and remained a major maritime hub through the Roman period. Within today’s castle-and-burg complex, the archaeological sequence spans from the Etruscan sanctuary/harbour landscape to Roman fortification and later occupation, before the site was redefined by the emergence of the medieval fortified nucleus that still shapes the topography. By the 10th–11th century, the fortified complex takes on the recognisable “castle” form attested by later written references.

Archaeological work carried out during the major restoration programme (especially 2003–2009) treated the castle as a set of distinct internal sectors rather than a single excavation area. Fieldwork targeted multiple loci across the fortified compound: "Piazza della Torretta" / "Casa del Commendatore", the beach-access strip, "Piazza delle Due Chiese", "Casa del Nostromo", "Piazza della Rocca"," Casa della Legnaia", "La Buca", "Viale del Castello" and the "Grande Giardino".

For the early medieval horizon (c. 5th/6th to 10th century AD), the castle area preserves evidence for both continuity and transformation: a late-antique Christian focus is signalled by the palaeochristian church near Piazza della Rocca, dated around the mid-5th century (with sources also placing it between the later 5th and early 6th). 
Within the castle stratigraphy, early medieval re-use of earlier structures includes productive and domestic activities—most notably a grain-roasting oven installation documented at Casa del Nostromo—while burial evidence indicates an expanding medieval funerary landscape (with cemetery use continuing into the central Middle Ages). 

Bibliography: Enei et alii 2013

contexts.name: Cd "Casa del Nostromo" (early production area, later cementery)
contexts.description:
Within the castle’s internal articulation, the Casa del Nostromo area is a particularly instructive “micro-palimpsest”: excavation, documenting Roman phases (including architectural elements and high-quality surfaces), followed by late-antique/early-medieval re-uses. Finally, an extensive medieval cemetery installed itself above earlier structural remains. 

The archaeobotanical evidence discussed is tied to an early medieval productive installation, interpreted as a grain-roasting oven (forno per tostatura del frumento) set against earlier masonry and associated with a stratified sequence that includes a late-6th-century (post-560 AD) beaten surface and overlying activity/deposition connected to the oven’s use and disuse. Botanical sampling covered multiple stratigraphic units (26) and yielded hundreds of charred macroremains (seeds/fruits) dominated by cereal processing—especially free-threshing/naked wheat, with barley and smaller quantities of legumes and other food plants—consistent with an on-site chaîne opératoire of cleaning/roasting/handling crops in the early medieval occupation of the castle area.

Bibliography: Enei et alii 2013

contexts.name: Hadrian's Villa
contexts.description:
Hadrian’s Villa is a vast imperial residence created in the 2nd century AD on the Tiburtine plain near ancient Tibur (modern Tivoli), conceived by Emperor Hadrian as a retreat from Rome and as an “ideal city” in which architecture, water, and landscape were fully integrated. 

Built mainly between AD 117/118 and 138, the complex brought together Roman engineering with eclectic cultural references (Greek, Roman and Egyptian motifs), expressed through a network of pavilions, baths, gardens, nymphaea and monumental water basins arranged on terraced platforms. The surviving remains comprise around 30 major buildings spread across roughly 120 hectares, making the villa closer in scale and complexity to an urban district than to a conventional country house. 

After antiquity the site underwent progressive abandonment, spoliation and reuse, while from the Renaissance onward it became a key focus for antiquarian collecting and archaeological research; today it is a UNESCO World Heritage property managed as an archaeological park, with ongoing stratigraphic investigations targeting specific sectors and their formation processes.

contexts.name: Antinoeion - rectangular planting trench
contexts.description:
The 2002–2004 excavations exposed a an Egyptianising tomb–temple complex connected with the divinised Antinous (drowned in AD 130) wich comprises a walled sacred precinct with two opposed rectangular temples on podia, a central square foundation interpreted as the obelisk base, and a large exedra at the opposite end; the bedrock (tuff) was cut extensively both for foundations and for garden installation. 

A the deep rectangular-section planting trench running almost continuously around the two temples (c. 1.20 m deep and 1.50 m wide), cut into the tuff and filled with fertile soil to support large ornamental trees (probabily palms, in order to evoke an “Egyptian” setting). The same garden scheme included shallower parallel trenches near the obelisk base (interpreted as beds/planters) and a coherent irrigation system with lead pipes branching from a main conduit fed by a small cistern upslope—important for understanding how the planted setting was engineered, even if sampling concentrated on the deep trench.

contexts.name: Antinoeion - late Repubblican cuts
contexts.description:
The 2002–2004 excavations exposed a an Egyptianising tomb–temple complex connected with the divinised Antinous (drowned in AD 130) wich comprises a walled sacred precinct with two opposed rectangular temples on podia, a central square foundation interpreted as the obelisk base, and a large exedra at the opposite end; the bedrock (tuff) was cut extensively both for foundations and for garden installation. 

In the area some antropic activity has been noted in the form of cuts in the tuff level wich shows a different (oblique) orientation. Some of these has proved to continue beneath the exedra’s foundations, therefore predating the Antinoeion’s construction (c. mid-2nd century AD). Among these earlier features is a rectangular pit (c. 3 × 3 m; preserved depth c. 0.30 m) containing a uniform soil layer with a charred plank trace along one side and an ash-rich patch with tuff chips and additional carbonised residues. The excavators interpret the ensemble, together with the surrounding quadrangular-section cuts, as evidence for cultivation/production installations belonging to the fundus of a nearby villa rustica predating Hadrian’s villa; a late Republican date (II–I century BC) is suggested by associated ceramic fragments and supported by radiocarbon dating of the charred wood studied archaeobotanically.

contexts.name: Isola Farnese (settlement)
contexts.description:
Isola Farnese is the plateau facing the city of Veii from the south, site of the medieval village. Excavations by the Soprintendenza and Sapienza University of Rome, outside the medieval borough and a few tens of metres from the church of S. Pancrazio, investigated c. 88 m² of a Final Bronze Age occupation deposit, with a hut of the early Final Bronze Age and a later structure with hearth, documenting the protohistoric settlement of the Veientine district before the rise of Veii.

Bibliography: Babbi, A. 2001. L'insediamento protostorico di Isola Farnese. Considerazioni sull'età del Bronzo finale nel distretto veiente. Atti XXIII Convegno di Studi Etruschi ed Italici; Celant, A. 2003. I resti paleobotanici. In Dalla capanna alla casa. I primi abitanti di Veio. Catalogo della mostra: 39–40.

contexts.name: Lunghezzina cemetery - tomb 2
contexts.description:
Tomb 2 is an artificial rock-cut chamber tomb heavily affected by later agricultural truncation, preserving only a shallow portion of the structure. The surviving layout includes an eastern access area/vestibule (irregular/triangular in plan) sloping toward the chamber and connecting to it through a narrow opening. The burial evidence is highly disturbed and poorly preserved, with very deteriorated bone fragments and teeth indicating at least one adult individual; the associated assemblage is modest, including scattered pottery fragments and a flint arrowhead. 

Charcoal/wood macro-remains from Tomb 2 were identified as alder (Alnus sp.) and maple (Acer sp.), recovered within the funerary deposits. 

Bibliography: Anzidei et al., La necropoli eneolitica di Lunghezzina (Roma) (2003); Anzidei e Carboni 2020, "Roma prima del mito".

contexts.name: grave 5
contexts.site: Montalto di Castro - Chiesa di San Sisto
contexts.description:
Grave 5 belongs to the group of small pit-type graves (3–7) cut into the cocciopesto floor after the main hypogeal/ossuary phase. Grave 5 is considered later than the other pit graves and was closed with bricks and mortar that disrupted the floor’s uniformity; part of the burial was removed when 18th-century cellar excavations cut through the stratigraphy.

Grave 5 is one of the pit-burials whose coffin wood survives as mineralized traces around nails and was identified as alder (Alnus sp.), in contrast with the poplar which seems to be used in the older crypt burial.

Bibliography: Sadori e Sabato 2009

contexts.name: tomb 1
contexts.site: Montalto di Castro - Chiesa di San Sisto
contexts.description:
Tomb 1 is a rock-cut hypogeum close to the church entrance, on the right aisle: an irregular rectangular chamber reached by a narrow stair, with an ossuary in the middle and two symmetric deposition platforms. The burial space was disturbed, but the excavation still documented multiple juvenile/child individuals and a set of devotional grave goods (e.g., rosary elements, a bronze crucifix, medals with saints).

The archaeobotanical finds belong to this funerary assemblage and to coffin/jewellery elements: poplar wood (Populus sp.) identified on nails/splinters from coffin remains; a necklace of birch wood beads (Betula sp.) threaded on wire; and an exceptional jasmine head-crown (Jasminum sp.), interpreted as part of funerary ritual display near children’s bodies.

Bibliography: Sadori e Sabato 2009

contexts.description:
Globular 'olletta' with four protrusions. contexts.name: Vessel 38
contexts.description:
Ovoid vessel with corded decoration. One of the pottery vessels recovered from the collapsed occupation layers of the submerged Gran Carro settlement (mostly found in an inclined position) and analysed by Fundurulic et al. (2022); the cereal-bearing vessels are typologically dated to the late 10th–9th century BC (Early Iron Age 1A, Villanovan). It contained a charred agglomeration of broomcorn millet fused into a lump shaped like the vessel base, interpreted as an intentional gathering of millet (storage or ritual). The lump was AMS-dated to 2847 ± 45 BP (LTL21223), 1195–899 cal BC (2σ), the only directly dated millet sample from the site.

contexts.name: Valentano - Santa Maria (settlement)
contexts.description:
The church of Santa Maria stands within the medieval core of Valentano, an urban setting that was heavily reshaped in the early 16th century during the Farnese reorganisation of the town after the 1510 fire. In the written sources, the church is securely attested only from the first half of the 16th century onward, with major architectural interventions (including an 18th-century rebuilding campaign in 1736–1744) and other documented events such as a collapse recorded in 1566. 

Archaeologically, a 2009 excavation reached, beneath the medieval floor levels, a compact cluster of structures dated on preliminary ceramic grounds to the late 13th–early 14th century AD. The earliest stratigraphic units belong to daily-use installations such as pits/silos and wells, while the later units relate to the church itself and to its construction phases, such as two bell-casting pits and an internal burial zone of prenatal/perinatal inhumations.

Bibliography: F. Rossi, G. Velluti 2014, Lo scavo della Chiesa di Santa Maria a Valentano, in Atti del convegno Etruria in progress. La ricerca archeologica in Etruria Meridionale, Roma, pp. 233 - 237.

contexts.name: Well/silo USS 162/164
contexts.description:
Under the church floor, in the W-SW area of the church, a conical pit-silo (US 164) was found. Below an upper arrangement interpreted as “alarii”-type elements composed of stones and reused ceramic fragments (US 162), were a fill (US 163) rich in carbonised botanical remains. It was probabily a storage silos belonging to a phase earlier than the church construction. The final infill then captured a concentrated snapshot of plant processing and disposal in the late 13th–early 14th century horizon. 

The assemblage is dominated by cereals and legumes, with associated weeds and fruit remains which seems consistent with mixed crop-processing residues rather than a single “clean” stored batch.

Bibliography: F. Rossi, G. Velluti 2014, Lo scavo della Chiesa di Santa Maria a Valentano, in Atti del convegno Etruria in progress. La ricerca archeologica in Etruria Meridionale, Roma, pp. 233 - 237.

contexts.name: SE Well - USS 40 (cut)/42&46 (fills)
contexts.description:
A large well (or well-like installation) US 40 belongs to the same late 13th–early 14th century activity horizon beneath the church. Two abandonment/infilling units (USS 42 and 46) were sampled for anthracology, providing evidence for fuelwood selection and local woodland exploitation associated with the occupation that preceded (or immediately accompanied) the earliest church phase. The charcoal spectrum suggest opportunistic use of nearby mixed oak woodland resources.

Bibliography: F. Rossi, G. Velluti 2014, Lo scavo della Chiesa di Santa Maria a Valentano, in Atti del convegno Etruria in progress. La ricerca archeologica in Etruria Meridionale, Roma, pp. 233 - 237.

contexts.name: Rectangular pit (US 39) with chestnut plank (US 48)
contexts.description:
A long uncharred chestnut plank (US 48) was recovered from the bottom of a rectangular pit (US –39). Unlike the securely late-medieval deposits, this element lacks decisive archaeological dating evidence, and has been tentatively linked to later interventions (hypothetically 16th or 19th century), pending independent dating approaches.

Bibliography: F. Rossi, G. Velluti 2014, Lo scavo della Chiesa di Santa Maria a Valentano, in Atti del convegno Etruria in progress. La ricerca archeologica in Etruria Meridionale, Roma, pp. 233 - 237.

contexts.name: Bell-casting pit – USS 77/78
contexts.description:
SE Bell-casting pit US –78 (associated deposit US 77)

One of two bell-casting pits belonging to the church’s building phase, the other one lying in the in the NW area of the Curch (US –109). The SE pit, here described, preserved internal firing features consistent with repeated casting operations. Within this operational setting, a charred stake from US 77 (a fill linked to the bell-casting installation) was analysed as part of the anthracological study. 

The stake was identified as an oak with ring-porous wood, probably Quercus sect. Cerris, consistent with the use of robust, locally available timbers in workshop/structural elements connected with casting activity.

Bibliography: F. Rossi, G. Velluti 2014, Lo scavo della Chiesa di Santa Maria a Valentano, in Atti del convegno Etruria in progress. La ricerca archeologica in Etruria Meridionale, Roma, pp. 233 - 237.

contexts.name: Valentano - Rocca Farnese (settlement)
contexts.description:
Rocca Farnese occupies the highest point of Valentano’s historic centre and preserves the long-term transformation of a medieval defensive stronghold into a Farnese residential palace. The site entered Farnese control in the mid-14th century (1354) and was progressively remodelled across the 15th–16th centuries: late-Quattrocento works include the creation of the so-called “Cortile d’Amore” for the 1488 marriage celebrations of Angelo Farnese and Lella Orsini, while further early-16th-century interventions—linked to the palace’s peak as an aristocratic residence—are attributed to the building phase associated with Pier Luigi Farnese and Gerolama Orsini and to designs by Antonio da Sangallo the Younger (e.g., architectural elements around portals and the well-head). In institutional terms, the Rocca reflects Valentano’s role within the wider Farnese dominion in northern Latium (the later Duchy of Castro landscape), before subsequent reuses and conversions in the post-Farnese centuries. 

Bibliography: Sadori, L.,_Celauro, F.,_Gobbi, E.,_Masi, A.,_Paganelli, M.,_Petitti, P.,_Rossi, F.,_Sabato, D._2013_A Medieval-Renaissance picture of common and aristocratic use of plants at Valentano (northern Latium, central Italy)_Abstract IWGP_156

contexts.name: Lago di Bolsena - Isola Bisentina (underwater)
contexts.description:
Lake Bolsena has yielded two Bronze Age monoxylous dugout canoes, one of which lies on the lakebed near Monte Bisenzio (Capodimonte, Viterbo), an area where surveys at Monte Bisenzio and on the Isola Bisentina document occupation from the Late Bronze Age to the Early Iron Age. The boats were studied for wood identification and radiocarbon dating by Calderoni et al. (1996); one of them was later recovered and prepared for display, while the other was left in situ.

contexts.name: US 814
contexts.description:
SU 814, one of the depositional layers of the 'deposito votivo reiterato' in area gamma, the Archaic south-western extension of the 'complesso monumentale'. The deposit lies immediately outside the north-eastern corner of the area, protected by an angled wall, and consists mainly of impasto ollae placed at different times below and above a tile, with faunal remains (including an ox scapula) and charred and mineralised plant remains (cereals, poppy, fig; oilseeds such as Camelina and grape pips are also reported). A chthonic character has been proposed for the cult.

contexts.name: alpha - olla 1
contexts.description:
Olla 1 of the foundation deposit in area alpha, on the western side of the 'complesso monumentale': a pair of impasto ollae set beneath an Archaic masonry wall, dated with the wall to the second half of the 6th–early 5th century BC. Both ollae and the surrounding soil show signs of in-situ burning. The mineralised plant remains, rich in chaff, include wheat, barley, emmer, einkorn and spelt (the first record of spelt at Tarquinia), lentil, grape, fig and elder; they are interpreted as the residue of a ritual action (possibly a lustration with liquids) rather than as stored offerings. The deposit is a 'closed' deposit of a type common on the Civita.

contexts.name: Pit 27 - Medieval level
contexts.description:
A smaller refuse feature in the pit cluster behind the proto-palace. It belongs to the Early group (broadly c. 1150–1390), i.e. deposits accumulated and were backfilled at some point before the major late-14th-century clearance episode. It also yelded faunal remains, though modest compared to the main pits.

Bibliography: Clark et al. 1989. "The Food Refuse of an Affluent Urban Household in the Late Fourteenth Century:
Faunal and Botanical Remains from the Palazzo Vitelleschi, Tarquinia (Viterbo)". In: Papers of the British School at Rome , 1989, Vol. 57 (1989), pp. 200-321.

contexts.name: Pit 179 - medieval level
contexts.description:
It belongs to the Early group (broadly c. 1150–1390), i.e. deposits accumulated and were backfilled at some point before the major late-14th-century clearance episode. It also yelded a substantial faunal assemblage within the “early” horizon.

Bibliography: Clark et al. 1989. "The Food Refuse of an Affluent Urban Household in the Late Fourteenth Century:
Faunal and Botanical Remains from the Palazzo Vitelleschi, Tarquinia (Viterbo)". In: Papers of the British School at Rome , 1989, Vol. 57 (1989), pp. 200-321.

contexts.name: Pit 4 - medieval levels
contexts.description:
One of the pits demonstrably filled concurrently with Pit 181 (and Pit 9) during the major late-14th-century clearance. It belongs to the Main group (labelled ~c. 1390) and is part of the same corridor/backyard system behind the proto-palace—sealed before/around the creation of the narrow street between Areas D and A3.

Bibliography: Clark et al. 1989. "The Food Refuse of an Affluent Urban Household in the Late Fourteenth Century:
Faunal and Botanical Remains from the Palazzo Vitelleschi, Tarquinia (Viterbo)". In: Papers of the British School at Rome , 1989, Vol. 57 (1989), pp. 200-321.

contexts.name: Pit 181 - medieval & Renaissence levels
contexts.description:
Pit 181 is the most complex and stratified of the pits, with distinct depositional episodes spanning the late medieval / early Renaissance transition and anchoring the site’s phasing.

Early deposits — Medieval (pre-1390): the earliest layers of Pit 181 fall in the Early group (within c. 1150–1390), evidenced in part by the associated numismatic horizon for the earliest deposits. 

Main filling — Renaissance (post-1390; “Main phase” ~c. 1390): the principal backfill belongs to the site’s major clearance episode, tightly dated by coins/seals to shortly after 1382 and plausibly within a decade of 1390; it is archaeologically linked to other pits of this phase (notably 4 and 9). 

Latest deposits — Renaissance (~c. 1400?–1436?): these additions belongs to a distinct layer, following the one just mentioned but still prior to the start of Vitelleschi’s palace works (1436).

Bibliography: Clark et al. 1989. "The Food Refuse of an Affluent Urban Household in the Late Fourteenth Century:
Faunal and Botanical Remains from the Palazzo Vitelleschi, Tarquinia (Viterbo)". In: Papers of the British School at Rome , 1989, Vol. 57 (1989), pp. 200-321.

contexts.name: Pit 9 - Renaissence levels
contexts.description:
One of the pits demonstrably filled concurrently with Pit 181 (and Pit 4) during the major late-14th-century clearance. It belongs to the Main group (labelled ~c. 1390) and is part of the same corridor/backyard system behind the proto-palace—sealed before/around the creation of the narrow street between Areas D and A3. 

Pit 9 was very rich in finds and ecofacts, with numismatic evidence anchoring its chronology. Coins finds in the pits places the filling shortly after 1382 and very likely around c. 1390, with no coins later than 1400 supporting a short time-window for deposition. 

Bibliography: Clark et al. 1989. "The Food Refuse of an Affluent Urban Household in the Late Fourteenth Century:
Faunal and Botanical Remains from the Palazzo Vitelleschi, Tarquinia (Viterbo)". In: Papers of the British School at Rome , 1989, Vol. 57 (1989), pp. 200-321.

contexts.name: Edificio β - US 223/13 - inside olla GR_C1
contexts.sourceDating: (end of the fourth century BCE to the beginning of the third century BCE
contexts.description:
SU 223/13, contents of olla GR_C1. Gravisca, the harbour of Tarquinia, hosted an emporic sanctuary founded at the end of the 7th century BC where Greek merchants traded under divine protection. The olla, deposited in the well of building β, contained carbonised seeds and charcoal selected after the burning of the offerings; its walls show no thermal alteration, indicating that the burnt remains were placed in it afterwards.

Signs of the sacred at the sanctuary of Gravisca, Italy: reconstruction of an Etruscan ritual through a multidisciplinary approach. contexts.name: Edificio β
contexts.sourceDating: (end of the fourth century BCE to the beginning of the third century BCE
contexts.description:
Gravisca, the harbour of Tarquinia, hosted an emporic sanctuary founded at the end of the 7th century BC where Greek merchants traded under divine protection. In building β, a well investigated in 2013 (first excavated in 1972) was used in the final phase of the sanctuary (end of the 4th–beginning of the 3rd century BC) for a ritual deposition reconstructed by Patrizi et al. through stratigraphy, archaeobotany and lipid residue analysis. Fruit, cereal and legume offerings (bread/durum wheat, broad bean, grape and pomegranate, the latter pointing to an autumn ceremony) were burned, probably inside amphora GR_C3; charcoal and seeds were then selected and placed in ollae GR_C1 and GR_C2, meat was cooked and seasoned with oil and beehive products, and the vessels were deposited in the well. Lipid analysis also suggested the presence of garum, the earliest such evidence in the Mediterranean.

Bibliography: Patrizi, G., Rageot, M., Cafisso, S., Pennetta, A., Fiorini, L., De Benedetto, G.E., Spiteri, C., Fiorentino, G. 2025. Signs of the sacred at the sanctuary of Gravisca, Italy: reconstruction of an Etruscan ritual through a multidisciplinary approach. Archaeometry 67(1): 235–247. https://doi.org/10.1111/arcm.13005; Fiorini, L. 2022. Sacrifici di seppellimento nel santuario etrusco di Gravisca.

contexts.name: Mazzano Romano - Mola di Monte Gelato (sacred)
contexts.site: Mazzano Romano - Mola di Monte Gelato
contexts.description:
Mola di Monte Gelato lies in the Treia valley near Mazzano Romano, about 30 km north of Rome. It was excavated in 1986–1990 by the British School at Rome and the British Museum (T.W. Potter, A.C. King) as part of the long-term survey of southern Etruria, revealing an exceptionally rich stratigraphy. An Augustan villa (where dormice were eaten and eels were kept) was abandoned in the early 3rd century AD; after sporadic late Roman and early medieval occupation in a frontier zone exposed to Lombard incursions, the site became in the 9th century a fortified ecclesiastical centre with a church and baptistery, linked to a papal estate (domusculta), with an associated cemetery. Charred plant remains from Roman to medieval phases were studied by J.A. Giorgi.

Bibliography: Potter, T.W., King, A.C. 1997. Excavations at the Mola di Monte Gelato. A Roman and medieval settlement in South Etruria (Archaeological Monographs of the British School at Rome 11). London; Giorgi, J.A. 1997. The charred plant remains. In Potter & King 1997: 407–411; Potter, T.W., King, A.C. 1988. Scavi a Mola di Monte Gelato presso Mazzano Romano, Etruria meridionale: primo rapporto preliminare. Archeologia Medievale XV.

contexts.name: Gabii - Urban Area
contexts.description:
Gabii lies along the Via Prenestina, in a strategic position that linked the Tyrrhenian-facing world of Rome with inland Latium. The archaeological site includes the remains of the ancient city and the medieval church of San Primitivo, a reminder that the area continued to be reoccupied after antiquity. 

Before the historical remains, Gabii also preserves a long urban biography, with early settlement showing a multinodal community already active by the 8th century BC. In Areas C and D, excavations documented an elite residential-and-productive compound that evolves across the Iron Age and Archaic period, with built space, activity areas (including food-related production) and infant burials that articulate social differentiation and the symbolic use of domestic space. These early phases belong to the centuries before the later orthogonal plan that signals a mature urban layout.

As from IV/III century BC, the city shows a mature urban system (streets, blocks, major axes such as the Via Gabina, and monumental nodes), with substantial Roman-period buildings visibile in almost all excavations sectors. These buildings includes domestic and productive complexes fronting the Via Gabina and infrastructures and occupation horizons which persisted well into the Imperial period. The overall picture is therefore not one of a simple “rise and fall”, but of repeated reconfiguration, starting from an Iron age domestic setting and ending in a complex Roman settelment.

contexts.name: Tincu House
contexts.description:
The so-called "Tincu House" is the best-known excavated residence in Area B and represents a Mid-Republican urban dwelling inserted into Gabii’s later city fabric. Archaeologically, it is crucial because it preserves both standing architectural logic (a large townhouse plan) and the subfloor stratigraphy that explains how such a building was inserted into a pre-existing urban landscape—through major levelling and the management of earlier deposits. 

Ceramic and stratigraphic analysis place the initial construction (Phase 1) broadly between the second quarter and the middle of the 3rd century BC, after substantial levelling operations that incorporated residual earlier materials. The house then remained in use for roughly two centuries, undergoing modifications across subsequent phases. It is then a long-lived domestic investment mirroring, changing needs and the wider reorganisation of the city in the Republican period.

contexts.description:
The “Valle Santa” site was identified during along Via di Boccea, in the Veii hinterland. The overall use of the area spans a long timeframe (Archaic to Late Roman), with a specific funerary nucleus south of a natural canal comprising six “vestibule”/“tramite” rock-cut tombs dated from the end of the 6th to the beginning of the 4th century BC. 

Within this Archaic–Classical funerary district, all investigated burials follow an incineration rite. Cremated remains were placed inside ceramic containers, wrapped in cloth, or collected in perishable containers and set on the bottom of each niche; in at least two cases the cinerary containers seem to have been intentionally laid on their side. Ritual activity is also documented by burnt offerings and associated containers deposited in the tramite, sometimes including highly “qualifying” personal items (notably a bronze strigil). 

Bibliography: De Cristofaro, Matta, Sforzini 2015; Moricca, De Cristofaro, Ambrosini 2023.

contexts.name: Tomb V - vase 1
contexts.site: Roma - Via di Valle Santa nell'Agro Veientano
contexts.description:
Tomb V, vase no. 1: sediment from inside a ceramic vase (c. 1.5 l) of Tomb V, a single-burial tomb of the Archaic funerary nucleus whose cremated remains were collected in a column-krater. It is the richest carpological sample of the necropolis (51 remains), with naked wheat caryopses, cereal fragments, a legume cotyledon and a fig achene, interpreted as food offerings, plus weed seeds.

Bibliography: Moricca, C., De Cristofaro, A., Ambrosini, L. 2023. Archaeobotanical evidence of funerary plant offerings at the Southern Etrurian necropolis of 'Valle Santa nell'Agro Veientano' (Rome, Italy). Interdisciplinaria Archaeologica 14(1): 63–70; De Cristofaro, A., Matta, A., Sforzini, C. 2015.

contexts.name: Tomb XX a - SU 160
contexts.site: Roma - Via di Valle Santa nell'Agro Veientano
contexts.description:
Tomb XX is a two-burial (bisome) tomb, characterised archaeologically by an impasto olla used as cinerary container. The tomb was found in a condition suggesting limited later disturbance beyond gradual sediment infiltration. 

SU 160 is the unit explicitly tied to Tomb XXa, and it is also singled out as the richest SU in charcoal fragments within the analysed set.

Bibliography: De Cristofaro, Matta, Sforzini 2015; Moricca, De Cristofaro, Ambrosini 2023.

contexts.name: Tomb VI d - SU 45
contexts.site: Roma - Via di Valle Santa nell'Agro Veientano
contexts.description:
Tomb VI is a multi-burial tomb (polisome), used for several depositions within the same architectural unit. Burial VId is one of the depositions interpreted as having used a perishable container for the cremated remains, inferred from the flattened, regular lenses of bones and associated evidence. The broader funerary pattern includes burnt offerings and associated containers placed in the tramite in contact with or close to the sealing devices of the niches.

Bibliography: De Cristofaro, Matta, Sforzini 2015; Moricca, De Cristofaro, Ambrosini 2023.

contexts.name: Tomb XX a/b - SU 62/160 B
contexts.site: Roma - Via di Valle Santa nell'Agro Veientano
contexts.description:
Tomb XX a/b, SU 62/160, sample B: sediment from the deposit shared by burials a and b of the two-burial Tomb XX (SU 160 is tied to Tomb XX a and is the unit richest in charcoal of the analysed set). Charcoal only, from local oak pyre wood and possibly wooden containers.

Bibliography: Moricca, C., De Cristofaro, A., Ambrosini, L. 2023. Archaeobotanical evidence of funerary plant offerings at the Southern Etrurian necropolis of 'Valle Santa nell'Agro Veientano' (Rome, Italy). Interdisciplinaria Archaeologica 14(1): 63–70; De Cristofaro, A., Matta, A., Sforzini, C. 2015.

contexts.name: Tomb V - N.D.
contexts.site: Roma - Via di Valle Santa nell'Agro Veientano
contexts.description:
Tomb V belongs to the single-burial group within the Archaic funerary nucleus. The cremated remains were collected in a column-krater (cratere a colonnette), and the tramite also yielded evidence for ritual deposition of goods—most notably a bronze strigil placed as a personal, status-marked item within the passage area rather than inside the niche itself. 

Archaeobotanical sampling points include: 
(a) SU 27 (sediment context), 
(b) an additional sediment sample labelled N.D. 
(c) the filling of “Vase #1” (a ceramic vessel context). 

Bibliography: De Cristofaro, Matta, Sforzini 2015; Moricca, De Cristofaro, Ambrosini 2023.

contexts.name: Tomb XX b - SU 62
contexts.site: Roma - Via di Valle Santa nell'Agro Veientano
contexts.description:
Tomb XX b, SU 62: soil from the niche of burial b of Tomb XX, a two-burial (bisome) tomb in which the cremated remains of burial b were probably gathered in a perishable container. Charcoal only, with many deciduous oak (Quercus sect. Robur) fragments possibly from a wooden box holding the remains.

Bibliography: Moricca, C., De Cristofaro, A., Ambrosini, L. 2023. Archaeobotanical evidence of funerary plant offerings at the Southern Etrurian necropolis of 'Valle Santa nell'Agro Veientano' (Rome, Italy). Interdisciplinaria Archaeologica 14(1): 63–70; De Cristofaro, A., Matta, A., Sforzini, C. 2015.

contexts.name: Tomb XX b - SU 154
contexts.site: Roma - Via di Valle Santa nell'Agro Veientano
contexts.description:
Tomb XX is a two-burial (bisome) tomb. It contained cremated remains without a ceramic cinerary, suggesting that originally such remains were gathered in cloth or another perishable container. 

Bibliography: De Cristofaro, Matta, Sforzini 2015; Moricca, De Cristofaro, Ambrosini 2023.

contexts.name: Tomb VI a - Bucchero chalice
contexts.site: Roma - Via di Valle Santa nell'Agro Veientano
contexts.description:
Tomb VI is a multi-burial tomb (polisome), used for several depositions within the same architectural unit. Burial VIa is associated with a ceramic cinerary container (purified-ware olla with plate/lid) and sits within the broader pattern of niche deposition and sealing typical of these tombe a tramite.

Bibliography: De Cristofaro, Matta, Sforzini 2015; Moricca, De Cristofaro, Ambrosini 2023.

contexts.name: Tomb V - SU 27
contexts.site: Roma - Via di Valle Santa nell'Agro Veientano

contexts.name: Tomb XX a/b - SU 60/162
contexts.site: Roma - Via di Valle Santa nell'Agro Veientano
contexts.description:
Tomb XX is a two-burial (bisome) tomb. A sediment context that “belongs to Tomb XX, part a and part b,” i.e., a shared or stratigraphically linked deposit spanning both sub-burials. Two separate samples are listed from this combined context (62/160 A* and 62/160 B*), reflecting distinct sample pulls within the same dual-attributed unit.

Bibliography: De Cristofaro, Matta, Sforzini 2015; Moricca, De Cristofaro, Ambrosini 2023.

contexts.name: Vessel A
contexts.description:
The coarseware jug is labelled no. 4 in the archaeological illustrations as a “brocca in rozza terracotta”, the larger vessel that retained most sediment, and it was subsampled in 1-cm mechanical layers for analysis. 

Bibliography: Flavio Enei, Pyrgi sommersa. I risultati delle nuove indagini subacquee, in Annali della Fondazione per il Museo “Claudio Faina” XXV (2018), pp. 347–361; Flavio Enei, Storia e archeologia dei porti ceretani di Pyrgi e Castrum Novum alla luce delle recenti scoperte, in Il Mediterraneo e la Storia II. Seamen, Ports and Navigation (Acta Instituti Romani Finlandiae 45), 2017 (estratto), pp. 234–244.

contexts.name: Santa Severa - Pyrgi - temples (sacred)
contexts.description:
Pyrgi is the coastal port-sanctuary of Caere (Cerveteri), located at Santa Severa on the Tyrrhenian shore. The monumental sacred precinct developed as a major religious and political “interface” between Caere and maritime networks, and it remained in use through the archaic and classical periods (with later reworkings in the Hellenistic age). 

Within the sanctuary, the two best-known buildings are Temples B and A. Temple B is the earlier monument (late 6th century BC), while Temple A represents a subsequent phase (mid–5th century BC). The famous gold tablets connect the sanctuary to high-status dedicatory practices and to a broader Mediterranean religious horizon, while architectural terracottas and votive/ritual installations point to long-lived ceremonial activity in and around the temples.

Bibliography: Coccolini & Follieri 1980

contexts.name: West Well (Temple A)
contexts.description:
The “West Well” belongs to the same infrastructural/ritual system as the South Well and was likewise built in tuff blocks around 450–440 BC near Temple A. Its bottom lay at about 4 m depth, cut into an organogenic limestone lens interbedded within the clay. As with the South Well, excavation proceeded by 10 successive cuts, grouped into three main strata marking different moments in the well’s closure; the deeper Stratum III (cuts 5–10) contained the main concentration of preserved plant remains and had a thickness of about 2.50 m in the West Well.

Bibliography: Coccolini & Follieri 1980

contexts.name: South well (Temple A)
Roma - Horti Lamiani (settlement)
contexts.description:
The Horti Lamiani occupied a large landscaped property on the Esquiline, broadly corresponding to the modern area around Piazza Vittorio Emanuele II. The sector excavated beneath the ENPAM offices documents a long sequence of land use: early agricultural exploitation (Middle Republican), followed by pozzolana extraction (mid-Republican), and then the creation of an artificially terraced garden in the Augustan age, when this extra-mural zone became part of Rome’s “green ring” of elite horti. 

The archaeobotanical samples come primarily from the Early Imperial garden arrangements (Period 3), especially the reorganisation under Tiberius–Caligula (Phase 3.2), when new terraces, an irrigation network (lead pipes), and dense systems of planting holes and plant pots were installed—some of them ollae perforatae set within a flower bed. Later interventions include the Claudian sealing of earlier garden features (Phase 3.3) and Flavian drainage works (Phase 3.4). After the garden phase, the area was reconfigured again, including the creation of a courtyard and a richly decorated nymphaeum in the Severan period, with continued life into Late Antiquity. 

Bibliography: Serlorenzi, Mirella et al. 2023. Il necessario invisibile. Impastare, miscelare, cuocere e conservare: il ruolo delle ceramiche dagli Horti Lamiani. Bollettino di Archeologia On Line XIV (2023/2); Masi, Alessia et al. 2023 (online 2024). “The first extensive study of an Imperial Roman Garden in the city of Rome: integrated archaeobotanical analyses from Horti Lamiani.” Vegetation History and Archaeobotany; Ministero della Cultura, Museo Ninfeo (Horti Lamiani) (institutional page).

contexts.name: Planting holes
contexts.description:
The excavated Early Imperial garden was organised on artificial terraces created by cutting earlier deposits and retaining them with concrete walls (Augustan Phase 3.1). Across these levels, archaeologists recorded planting trenches and discrete planting holes arranged in regular patterns parallel to the terrace walls, often with tuff fragments placed at the bottom for drainage and to prevent waterlogging. 

In the main planting episode relevant to the sampled material (Tiberius–Caligula, Phase 3.2), the layout includes circular and square planting holes (roughly 0.05–0.20 m wide and 0.10–0.25 m deep), set singly or in double rows about 0.8–1 m from the terrace walls; tighter clusters of smaller holes close to some walls suggest differentiated planting (e.g., edging or low shrubs versus larger specimens). This phase is also linked to an irrigation system using lead pipes, implying managed watering for ornamental and/or productive plants within a highly curated garden design.

Bibliography: Serlorenzi, Mirella et al. 2023. Il necessario invisibile. Impastare, miscelare, cuocere e conservare: il ruolo delle ceramiche dagli Horti Lamiani. Bollettino di Archeologia On Line XIV (2023/2); Masi, Alessia et al. 2023 (online 2024). “The first extensive study of an Imperial Roman Garden in the city of Rome: integrated archaeobotanical analyses from Horti Lamiani.” Vegetation History and Archaeobotany; Ministero della Cultura, Museo Ninfeo (Horti Lamiani) (institutional page).

contexts.name: Filling deposits
Flower bed with ollae perforatae
contexts.description:
One particularly diagnostic garden installation of Phase 3.2 is a flower bed equipped with ollae perforatae: perforated ceramic pots set into the soil to hold plants while improving drainage and root aeration. In the ENPAM sector, multiple ollae perforatae were documented within a defined bed, alongside other container solutions (e.g., broken amphorae reused as flower pots) that point to intensive horticultural management and possibly the display/propagation of selected ornamentals or shrubs in a controlled substrate. 

These pots are central to the archaeobotanical programme: the published study explicitly ties many analysed sediments to the fill of smaller planting holes and to the ollae perforatae themselves, meaning that this “plant-pot area” provides a tightly contextualised window onto what was actually being cultivated (and how) during the Tiberius–Caligula redesign of the garden.

Bibliography: Serlorenzi, Mirella et al. 2023. Il necessario invisibile. Impastare, miscelare, cuocere e conservare: il ruolo delle ceramiche dagli Horti Lamiani. Bollettino di Archeologia On Line XIV (2023/2); Masi, Alessia et al. 2023 (online 2024). “The first extensive study of an Imperial Roman Garden in the city of Rome: integrated archaeobotanical analyses from Horti Lamiani.” Vegetation History and Archaeobotany; Ministero della Cultura, Museo Ninfeo (Horti Lamiani) (institutional page).

contexts.name: Fidene (prehistoric hut)
contexts.description:
The “Capanna di Fidene” is an Early Iron Age domestic structure excavated on the margins of ancient Fidenae, a strategic settlement controlling the Tiber corridor and the Via Salaria. The original hut—destroyed by an accidental fire around c. 800 BC survived archaeologically thanks to the charring and collapse of its timber elements, which sealed parts of the floor assemblage and preserved construction details (post settings, internal fittings, and traces of the superstructure). 

A key aspect of its importance is that the hut is not only an excavated plan, but a didactic/experimental reconstruction at 1:1 scale, built with materials and techniques consistent with the archaeological evidence and installed close to the original findspot (the excavated remains were then reburied for protection). This makes it one of the most tangible reference points in Rome for understanding Iron Age domestic architecture and daily life—from the structural logic of posts, walls and roofing to the organisation of internal space—while also serving as a public-facing “laboratory” for communicating protohistoric building practices.

Bibliography: Celant, De Santis, Merlo & De Grossi Mazzorin 1998, Una casa dell’età del Ferro: la capanna di Fidene; “Una capanna dell’età del Ferro: archeologia sperimentale a Fidene”, Scuole Musei in Comune Roma (web resource).

contexts.name: Charred plant remains
contexts.description:
The hut yielded a limited but informative set of plant macro-remains, likely carbonised in connection with the fire that destroyed the structure. The published list includes cereals (emmer and einkorn, barley, and Triticum aestivum), durum wheat, legumes, and a small number of grape seeds—evidence consistent with a mixed agro-pastoral economy and with storage/processing of staple crops in (or near) domestic space.

Bibliography: Celant, De Santis, Merlo & De Grossi Mazzorin 1998, Una casa dell’età del Ferro: la capanna di Fidene.

contexts.name: Vulci - Necropoli dell'Osteria (funerary)
contexts.description:
The Osteria necropolis lies in the 'Valle dell'Osteria', in the northern cemetery district of Vulci, explored by U. Ferraguti and R. Mengarelli in 1929–1931 and, in recent decades, by the Fondazione Vulci and the Soprintendenza, with new excavations of Orientalising and Archaic chamber tombs. Bioarchaeological studies of plant offerings deposited in the tombs were presented in the exhibition 'Principi immortali. Fasti dell'aristocrazia etrusca a Vulci' (2014).

Bibliography: Marchesini, M., Marvelli, S., Rizzoli, E. 2014. L'archeobotanica a Vulci. In Principi immortali. Fasti dell'aristocrazia etrusca a Vulci. Catalogo della mostra. Roma: 37–41; Carosi, S. La necropoli dell'Osteria a Vulci: un aggiornamento sulla storia delle ricerche. In Il vino dono degli dei. La Tomba 58 della necropoli dell'Osteria – Area C e la bioarcheologia a Vulci.

contexts.name: Campionamento della necropoli dell'osteria
contexts.description:
Archaeobotanical sampling of Orientalising-period tombs of the Osteria necropolis at Vulci, carried out by M. Marchesini, S. Marvelli and E. Rizzoli on plant offerings associated with the elite burials presented in 'Principi immortali' (2014).

Bibliography: Marchesini, M., Marvelli, S., Rizzoli, E. 2014. L'archeobotanica a Vulci. In Principi immortali. Fasti dell'aristocrazia etrusca a Vulci. Catalogo della mostra. Roma: 37–41; Carosi, S. contexts.name: Poggio Olivastro (settlement)
contexts.description:
Poggio Olivastro is a prehistoric settlement on the travertine plateau of Canino (Viterbo), excavated in 1991–1992 by the Museo Pigorini (G.M. Bulgarelli). The site, enclosed by an elliptical ditch of about 90 × 80 m, was frequented in several Neolithic phases, discussed in the light of radiocarbon dates by G. Belluomini (2004).

Bibliography: Bulgarelli, G.M. et al. 1995. L'insediamento preistorico di Poggio Olivastro (Canino, VT): campagne di scavo 1991–1992; Belluomini, G. 2004. Poggio Olivastro. Considerazioni sulle fasi di frequentazione neolitica alla luce delle recenti datazioni al radiocarbonio; Costantini, L. 2002. Italia centro-meridionale.

contexts.name: Grotta Misa
contexts.description:
Grotta Misa is a natural cave on the Fiora valley near Ischia di Castro (Viterbo), explored by L. Cardini in 1946 and excavated in 1947 by F. Rittatore Vonwiller and L. Cardini. It contained a Middle Bronze Age deposit with funerary use; surface material on the nearby plateau of Le Colle documents a settlement of the same period.

Bibliography: Catalogo Generale dei Beni Culturali (ICCD), scheda 'Grotta Misa' (ICCD13689616); Rittatore Vonwiller, F. 1951. Scoperte di età eneolitica e del bronzo nella Maremma tosco-laziale. contexts.name: Narce (undet.)
contexts.description:
Narce is a Faliscan settlement in the Treia valley, about 5 km south of Falerii (Civita Castellana), comprising three hills. The British School at Rome excavations directed by T.W. Potter in 1966–1971 documented the human occupation of the site from the Bronze Age (with settlement in the low areas along the Treia) to the Faliscan town, until its demise in the mid-3rd century BC.

Bibliography: Potter, T.W. 1976. A Faliscan town in South Etruria. Excavations at Narce 1966–71. London: British School at Rome; Costantini, L. 2002. Italia centro-meridionale. In Storia dell'agricoltura italiana I: 221–233.

contexts.name: Sorgente della Nova (undet.)
contexts.description:
Sorgenti della Nova is a protohistoric settlement on a tuff outcrop at the western edge of the province of Viterbo (comune di Farnese), where the Fosso La Nova marks the border with Tuscany. The c. 15 ha hill was stably occupied from the beginning of the Final Bronze Age 3, with terraced slopes and dwellings including a monumental ditch-house, and was frequented until the threshold of the Iron Age.

Bibliography: Gallo, V. The Memory of Places: the settlement of Sorgenti della Nova in the Etruscan period. The case study of Sector XII. Aristonothos; Costantini, L. 2002. Italia centro-meridionale. In Storia dell'agricoltura italiana I: 221–233.

contexts.name: Torrionaccio (settlement)
contexts.description:
Torrionaccio is a protohistoric hilltop settlement near Ancarano, along the route from Norchia to Tarquinia (Viterbo), excavated by S.M. Puglisi with S.M. Cassano and A. Manfredini (Sapienza University of Rome) and published in 1978. The excavation exposed occupation structures of the Final Bronze Age, with plant remains analysed by M. Follieri.

Bibliography: Puglisi, S.M., Cassano, S.M., Manfredini, A. 1978. Torrionaccio (Viterbo). Scavo di un abitato protostorico. Notizie degli Scavi di Antichità 32: 159–269 (with the plant remains by M. Follieri); Costantini, L. 2002. Italia centro-meridionale. In Storia dell'agricoltura italiana I: 221–233.

contexts.name: Sample D2 outside the bowl

contexts.name: San Giovenale (undet.)
contexts.description:
San Giovenale is an Etruscan settlement on a tuff plateau near Blera (Viterbo), excavated by the Swedish Institute of Classical Studies in Rome in 1956–1965. The plateau comprises two residential areas, the Acropolis (dominated by a medieval castle) and the Borgo, separated by a cut roadway, with the Vignale plateau linked by an Etruscan bridge. Occupation spans Bronze Age and Final Bronze Age huts, Iron Age oval huts, Orientalising and Archaic houses (rebuilt after an earthquake c. 550/530 BC) and later Hellenistic and medieval phases. Area B, on the Acropolis between the western façade of the castle and the moat, was excavated in 1957–1960 and yielded Bronze Age deposits, a rectangular tufa house, two Archaic cisterns and a 4th–3rd-century well.

Bibliography: Berggren, E., Berggren, K. 1981. San Giovenale II:2. Excavations in Area B, 1957–1960 (with appendices by H. Helbaek and C. Sorrentino). Stockholm; Olinder, B., Pohl, I. 1981. San Giovenale II:4. The semi-subterranean building in Area B. Stockholm.

contexts.name: Area B - Trincea a ovest rispetto al castello
contexts.description:
Trench west of the castle in Area B on the Acropolis of San Giovenale, part of the Swedish excavations of 1957–1960 (directed by E. Berggren, then by B.E. Thomasson and B. Olinder), which documented Bronze Age deposits beneath later Etruscan structures; the context is attributed to the Late Bronze Age. Plant remains were studied by H. Helbaek in an appendix to the Area B report.

Bibliography: Berggren, E., Berggren, K. 1981. San Giovenale II:2. Excavations in Area B, 1957–1960 (with appendices by H. Helbaek and C. Sorrentino). Stockholm; Olinder, B., Pohl, I. 1981. San Giovenale II:4. The semi-subterranean building in Area B. Stockholm.

contexts.name: Satricum (undet.)
contexts.description:
Satricum (Borgo Le Ferriere, Latina), c. 60 km south-east of Rome, is a Latin, later Volscian, settlement centred on an acropolis with the sanctuary of Mater Matuta. Systematically excavated by the University of Amsterdam since the late 1970s, it shows an Iron Age community of huts on the acropolis, the first buildings with stone foundations in the 7th century BC and the replacement of huts by houses during the 6th century, with Latin and Volscian necropoleis and votive deposits; habitation continued at least until the 3rd century BC.

Bibliography: Gnade, M. (ed.) 2007. Satricum. Trenta anni di scavi olandesi. Amsterdam; Bouma, J.W. et al. 1995. The economy of an early Latin settlement, Borgo Le Ferriere-Satricum, 800–200 BC; Costantini, L. 2002. Italia centro-meridionale. In Storia dell'agricoltura italiana I: 221–233.

contexts.name: Acquarossa (undet.)
contexts.description:
Acquarossa is an Etruscan town on a tufa plateau near Viterbo, close to Lake Bolsena, excavated by the Swedish Institute of Classical Studies in Rome in 1966–1978. The excavations revealed an Iron Age village of round and oval huts and a series of Etruscan houses inhabited from the late 8th century BC until shortly after the mid-6th century BC, when the town was suddenly abandoned; the monumental Zone F included porticoed buildings decorated with architectural terracottas. As the site was never built over, it is a key reference for Etruscan domestic architecture.

Bibliography: Lulof, P., Sepers, A. 2017. Acquarossa (Archeologia e Calcolatori 28.2); Costantini, L. 2002. Italia centro-meridionale. In Storia dell'agricoltura italiana I: 221–233.

contexts.name: Sant'Antonio - Cereveteri (funerary)
contexts.description:
The sanctuary of Sant'Antonio lies at the south-eastern access to the urban plateau of Caere (Cerveteri), where an ancient road climbed from the Fosso della Mola through a rock-cut 'via cava'. Excavations began in 1993 under M. Cristofani and M.A. Rizzo (CNR and Soprintendenza), with a parallel Cambridge team (V. Izzet) in 1995–1998.

Before the sanctuary, the area hosted pit inhumations of the 2nd millennium BC and a late Villanovan hut settlement. Two aligned Tuscan-type temples ('a' and the larger 'b') with a large altar between them face south-east; a basin filled with material down to c. 520–510 BC provides a terminus post quem for temple a (late 6th–early 5th century BC). Hercle is identified as the main deity (a cup by Euphronios and black-figure scenes of Hercle in the Gigantomachy). The area in front of the temples was restructured around the late 4th century BC; a bothros yielded offerings from the late 6th century to the early Hellenistic period, after which the sanctuary declined.

Bibliography: Izzet, V.E. 2000. The Etruscan sanctuary at Cerveteri, Sant'Antonio: preliminary report of excavations 1995–8 (with a contribution on the plant remains by C. Stevens). Papers of the British School at Rome 68: 321–335; Maggiani, A., Rizzo, M.A. 2005. Cerveteri. Le campagne di scavo in loc. Vigna Parrocchiale e S. Antonio. Atti XXIII Convegno di Studi Etruschi ed Italici.
