Atti XXIII Convegno di Studi Etruschi ed Italici.

contexts.name: Leopoli - Cencelle (settlement)
contexts.description:
Cencelle (medieval Leopoli) is a planned hilltop town founded in the 9th century in the territory of Tarquinia, created within the wider Carolingian–papal response to instability along the Tyrrhenian coast. The settlement developed a structured street grid and masonry buildings, and remained occupied for centuries, before major destruction and progressive abandonment in the late medieval period.

Sector III is one of the excavated urban blocks where the town’s late-medieval life is particularly clear: it combines domestic units with spaces linked to production and storage, set along paved streets and near a gate-facing axis. The excavated sequence includes substantial late activity and an abandonment episode connected with a destructive fire between the late 14th and early 15th century.

Within Sector III, the sampled environments (A, B, C, E, F, H, K, P, R) belong to a compact neighbourhood including: an open/access space (A) tied to a granary (B); a smith’s workshop at a street junction (C–H) with water-management features; a small domestic building (E) served by an associated open court (F); and a larger service/farm building (P–R) opening onto the paved street and used for storage and the keeping/management of working animals.

Bibliography: Stasolla, F. R. (ed.), "Leopoli-Cencelle: Il quartiere Sud-Orientale".

contexts.name: Sector III – Room R (stable/storage compartment within P–R)
contexts.description:
In Sector III, Room R is the best-defined “service” space within the P–R complex: part of its floor included a well-paved corner beside a raised element interpreted as support for an animal manger, and the destruction layers produced evidence consistent with the management of working animals and farm equipment. Assemblages include numerous metal items linked to agricultural activity and animal handling (e.g., horseshoes/donkey shoes, chain rings/fittings), and the building also contained (or supported above) substantial cereal reserves, before being destroyed by the late-14th/early-15th-century fire that contributed to the abandonment of the quarter.

Bibliography: Stasolla, F. R. (ed.), "Leopoli-Cencelle: Il quartiere Sud-Orientale".

contexts.name: Sector II - US 555
contexts.description:
US 555 in Sector II of Leopoli-Cencelle, the medieval town founded by Pope Leo IV in the 9th century in the territory of Tarquinia. Sector II lies in the south-eastern quarter, near the eastern gate, where the main road splits into stepped streets; its houses face an open space and the excavations documented a cistern, rock-cut traces and post holes of wooden buildings, including a semi-elliptical structure with a rock-cut pit probably used for grain storage; the sequence spans the 9th–16th centuries AD.

Bibliography: Stasolla, F.R. (ed.) 2012. Leopoli-Cencelle. Il quartiere sud-orientale. Spoleto: Fondazione CISAM.

contexts.name: Sector III - US 1318 - Ambiente R
contexts.description:
US 1318 in Room R of Sector III at Leopoli-Cencelle, the best-defined service space of the large building P–R, with a well-paved corner beside a raised element interpreted as the support of an animal manger (stable). The destruction layers relate to the fire that ended the use of this late-medieval block (9th–15th century AD sequence).

Bibliography: Stasolla, F.R. (ed.) 2012. Leopoli-Cencelle. Il quartiere sud-orientale. Spoleto: Fondazione CISAM.

contexts.name: Sector III - undet. (Leopoli Cencelle)
contexts.description:
Generic sampling unit from Sector III of Leopoli-Cencelle, an urban block of the south-eastern quarter combining dwellings, a granary, a smithy and service buildings along paved streets, excavated in 1994–1999 by the École française de Rome; 9th–15th century AD.

Bibliography: Stasolla, F.R. (ed.) 2012. Leopoli-Cencelle. Il quartiere sud-orientale. Spoleto: Fondazione CISAM.

contexts.name: Sector III – Room B (granary)
contexts.description:
In Sector III, Room B is explicitly interpreted as a granary, accessed from above via a trapdoor and connected to the adjacent circulation/access space. The arrangement implies controlled storage (and likely protection) of foodstuffs within a dense urban setting, consistent with the broader evidence for provisioning and agricultural logistics inside the block.

Bliography: Stasolla, F. R. (ed.), "Leopoli-Cencelle: Il quartiere Sud-Orientale".

contexts.name: Sector III – Room C (part of the smith’s workshop complex)
contexts.description:
In Sector III, Room C forms one of the two adjoining spaces of a blacksmith’s workshop positioned at a junction of paved streets. The workshop’s placement—immediately on a movement corridor—fits a neighbourhood where craft activity and circulation were closely intertwined, and the building includes practical adaptations for managing runoff.

Bibliography: Stasolla, F. R. (ed.), "Leopoli-Cencelle: Il quartiere Sud-Orientale".

contexts.name: Sector III – Room F (open court linked to Room E)
contexts.description:
In Sector III, Room F is an unroofed quadrangular court associated with Room E and containing access elements (including a stair run) for the upper storey. As a yard-like space within a tight block, it likely supported everyday outdoor tasks (handling goods, maintenance, minor craft), and it is also described as a place where animal-related and tool-storage functions could occur within the sector.

Bibliography: Stasolla, F. R. (ed.), "Leopoli-Cencelle: Il quartiere Sud-Orientale".

contexts.name: Sector III – Room H (forge area)
contexts.description:
In Sector III, Room H is the core working space of the smithy/forge, paired with Room C. The workshop is characterised by unusually robust perimeter construction and a built rainwater-drain channel that discharged directly onto the street—an infrastructure choice consistent with hot-working activities and frequent cleaning/water use in a confined urban plot.

Bibliography: Stasolla, F. R. (ed.), "Leopoli-Cencelle: Il quartiere Sud-Orientale".

contexts.name: Sector III – Room K (sampled room within the block)
contexts.description:
In Sector III, Room K is one of the sampled environments inside the excavated block. While it is less prominently described in the published architectural synopsis than the granary, forge, and large service building, it belongs to the same late-medieval occupational fabric and is treated as part of the domestic/service spaces from which archaeobotanical samples were collected.

The exact location of this room was not possibile to obtain from the bibliography source.

Bibliography: Stasolla, F. R. (ed.), "Leopoli-Cencelle: Il quartiere Sud-Orientale".

contexts.name: Sector III – Room A (access/open space associated with storage)
contexts.description:
productive function areaIn Sector III, Room A is described as a heavily reworked space organised around an open area and functionally connected with nearby storage installations. Its late reorganisation is part of the broader intensification of the block in the final occupation phases, and it is also one of the areas affected by the fire that marks the end of use of this quarter.

Bliography: Stasolla, F. R. (ed.), "Leopoli-Cencelle: Il quartiere Sud-Orientale".

contexts.name: Sector III – Room E (small domestic unit)
contexts.description:
In Sector III, Room E is interpreted as a small dwelling (roughly a single-room ground plan) equipped with an internal hearth and traces for domestic fittings. Its modest size and likely vertical development (upper floor accessed via stairs) fit a late-medieval urban household unit inserted into the block beside craft and service spaces.

Bibliography: Stasolla, F. R. (ed.), "Leopoli-Cencelle: Il quartiere Sud-Orientale".

contexts.name: Sector III – Room P (part of the large service/farm building P–R)
contexts.description:
In Sector III, Room P belongs to the large building complex P–R that fronts the paved street with a double arched entrance and internal circulation between compartments. The building combines substantial access control with internal fixtures (including a large circular trachyte feature) and is best interpreted as a multifunctional service structure (storage + work/handling areas), closely tied to the agricultural economy implied by the associated finds.

Bibliography: Stasolla, F. R. (ed.), "Leopoli-Cencelle: Il quartiere Sud-Orientale".

contexts.name: Palatino: Area 4, Area 5, Settore 9
contexts.description:
Areas 4 and 5 and Sector 9 were grouped together are the three excavation/sampling units from which Prof.ssa Laura Motta (2002) drew its archaeobotanical macroremains samplings representive of the northern slope of the Palatine Hill early profile (spanning the 8th–6th centuries BC), also capturing different micro-settings within the same settlement system (inside the fortification, movement/circulation surfaces, and wall-related occupation deposits). 

Area 4 lies inside the fortification and is described as being composed mainly of occupation layers and postholes, with samples taken from occupation surfaces and related deposits (including pit/hole backfills and build-up layers). 

Area 5 includes the earliest (8th-century BC) contexts in the dataset, but most contexts are linked to a later (7th-century BC) small gravel trackway/road surface, with many samples coming from backfills of pits and holes and associated occupation/build-up deposits. 

Sector 9 is characterised by a sequence of linear features (E–W aligned) interpreted as wall-related elements; the associated deposits include occupation layers, with features such as hearths, a hut, and numerous postholes, making it particularly informative for activity areas connected to fortification-related spaces

contexts.name: Capena - Lucus Feroniae
contexts.sourceDating: post 208 BC - beginning of the 2nd century BC-phase 1
contexts.description:
Lucus Feroniae, discovered in 1952 at the locality of Bambocci, hosts one of the most important sanctuaries of the goddess Feronia in antiquity. Frequented as early as the Iron Age, it developed from the Archaic period onward, as evidenced by the materials found in the votive deposit. Rebuilt after the sack by Hannibal, the sanctuary is currently known only through the excavations of the temple constructed from the last decades of the 3rd century BCE, at the same time as the emergence of an initial settlement layout nearby. The sanctuary was abandoned and the area became a colony between the Sullan and Caesarian periods, but only during the principate of Augustus did it experience significant growth. The settlement was abandoned during Late Antiquity and became a source of spolia, with the construction of numerous lime kilns. At present, only some areas of the colony have been excavated (the forum, part of the sanctuary, the amphitheatre, and the baths), while others have been investigated through non-invasive methods (Kay et al. 2018).

Source: MOSI record ID SABAP-VT-EM_2024_tirocinio_Balzerani_36, author Lorenzo Balzerani (content manager: Lorenzo Balzerani), compiled in 2024, https://gna.cultura.gov.it
(original in Italian; personal translation).

contexts.name: Lucus Feroniae - ?
contexts.sourceDating: post 208 BC - beginning of the 2nd century BC-phase 1
contexts.description:
Unspecified context of the temple of Feronia, dated after 208 BC–beginning of the 2nd century BC. The 2000–2010 excavations of the temple of Feronia investigated the foundations of the sacred building erected after Hannibal's sack (post 208 BC–early decades of the 2nd century BC), including the creation of a bothros, ritual consecration deposits in the back sector of the cella and foundation deposits of vases; the masonry was later systematically robbed (late 3rd/early 4th–11th century AD). Charcoal from these contexts provided the first anthracological data from the sanctuary of the sacred grove (Primavera & Porta 2019).

Bibliography: Primavera, M., Porta, M. 2019. Il bosco sacro e le analisi archeobotaniche: i primi dati antracologici dal santuario di Lucus Feroniae. In Benedettini, M.G., Sgubini Moretti, A.M. (eds), Un grande santuario interetnico: Lucus Feroniae. Scavi 2000–2010. Pisa: ETS, vol. 2: 883–888.

The 2000–2010 excavations of the temple of Feronia investigated the foundations of the sacred building erected after Hannibal's sack (post 208 BC–early decades of the 2nd century BC), including the creation of a bothros, ritual consecration deposits in the back sector of the cella and foundation deposits of vases; the masonry was later systematically robbed (late 3rd/early 4th–11th century AD). Charcoal from these contexts provided the first anthracological data from the sanctuary of the sacred grove (Primavera & Porta 2019).

contexts.name: Roma - Basilica Iulia - Navata centrale della Basilica Iulia
contexts.description:
The Basilica Iulia occupies the southern side of the Roman Forum. In 1960–1964 L. Fabbrini (Soprintendenza Archeologica di Roma) excavated two large areas beneath the Augustan floor, bringing to light the remains of Caesar's basilica, the Basilica Sempronia (169 BC), a large atrium house of the 4th century BC and traces of a 5th-century BC building. The Basilica Iulia Project (Parco archeologico del Colosseo, CNR and Sapienza University of Rome) has published these excavations, reconstructing the sequence of the area from the first frequentation at the dawn of the Republic, through the mid-Republican reorganisation of the quarter, to the Augustan building site, with archaeometric, archaeozoological and archaeobotanical studies.

Bibliography: Primavera, M. 2023. I resti vegetali dai contesti pre-augustei e augustei. In Basilica Iulia I. Gli scavi di Laura Fabbrini (1960–1964). Strutture, stratigrafie e materiali dalla prima età repubblicana alla costruzione augustea. Istanbul: Ege Yayınları: 497–502.; Falzone, S., Galli, M., Ismaelli, T. 2019. Rinvenimento di frammenti di primo stile dagli scavi Carettoni-Fabbrini della Basilica Iulia. Scienze dell'Antichità.

contexts.name: Roma - Palatino - NE area
contexts.description:
The sector between the north-eastern slope of the Palatine, the Velia and the western side of the Colosseum valley was investigated by the Department of Sciences of Antiquity of Sapienza University of Rome (C. Panella, A.F. Ferrandes) from 2001 onwards. The research documented an Iron Age hut settlement along the present Via Sacra, a sanctuary on the southern slope of the Velia with 'well-cases' of the mid–later 8th century BC, and a second sacred area between valley and hill identified with the Curiae Veteres – the civic sanctuary attributed by tradition to Romulus, frequented from the 8th century BC to the mid/late 4th century AD – together with Archaic and Republican residential blocks and a dense road network. The mid-Republican (4th–3rd century BC) stratigraphy has been published by Ferrandes (2024).

Bibliography: Ferrandes, A.F. 2024. Strade, santuari e domus tra Palatino e Velia nella media età repubblicana (IV–III secolo a.C.). 1. Stratigrafie, contesti, ricostruzioni (with texts by C. Armenio, E. Brienza, L. Fornaciari, A. Masi, D. Nonnis). Roma: Quasar; Armenio, C., Masi, A. 2024. In Ferrandes 2024: 501–506; Panella, C. et al. 2019. Curiae Veteres. Nuovi dati sulla frequentazione del santuario in età tardo-repubblicana. Scienze dell'Antichità 25.1.

contexts.name: Atrium Vestae
contexts.description:
The Atrium Vestae, the residence of the Vestal Virgins, lies at the eastern edge of the Roman Forum between the Regia and the Palatine. Together with the temple of Vesta and the Regia it formed the religious centre of the Roman state until the fire of AD 64, which largely destroyed all three buildings. The American Academy in Rome, with the Soprintendenza Archeologica di Roma, excavated the area sacra of Vesta in 1987–1996 under R.T. Scott, establishing a reliable chronology for the complex from Iron Age huts and Archaic wells through the Republican and Imperial phases of the Atrium to its medieval reoccupation. Charred plant remains from the excavation were studied by L. Costantini and J.A. Giorgi.

Bibliography: Scott, R.T. (ed.) 2009. Excavations in the Area Sacra of Vesta (1987–1996). Memoirs of the American Academy in Rome, Suppl. 8. Ann Arbor; Costantini, L., Giorgi, J.A. 2009. The charred plant remains. In Scott (ed.) 2009: 125–151; Costantini, L., Giorgi, J. 2001. Charred plant remains of the Archaic period from the Forum and Palatine. Journal of Roman Archaeology 14: 239–248.

contexts.name: Middle Chalcolithic village of Le Cerquete–Fianello (Maccarese)
contexts.description:
Le Cerquete–Fianello is a well-preserved Middle Chalcolithic (Copper Age) village on the Roman coastal plain, set on a low sandy rise at the edge of the former Lago di Maccarese, protected by overlying lagoon deposits that helped seal the archaeological horizon. The site was identified during broader landscape surveys and then excavated in annual campaigns (1993–2002), revealing a village of c. 1 ha (with c. 1,000 m² excavated). 

The excavated sector includes five huts (A–E), a palisade enclosing part of the settlement, pits and peripheral activity zones. A stratigraphic/structural sequence has been proposed within the village’s life: an earlier layout with the palisade and huts A–C, followed by phases in which some pits cut earlier features, and a later episode in which hut E is built after the infilling/obliteration of earlier pits—yet the radiocarbon dataset is consistent with one broad occupation episode within the Middle Chalcolithic. 

At the south-eastern edge, a marginal zone concentrates pits, pozzetti, hearths and dense deposits, including a ritual 'pozzetto' with an intentionally arranged horse burial (with two dog puppies separated by a clay lens), and nearby funerary evidence (including a fetal burial in a vessel and other burials/crania). 
Radiocarbon dates place the occupation broadly between c. 3550–2920 BC (cal.), with samples tied to hut A, pits, postholes, and the ritual equid burial. 

Anthracological work on charcoals from the excavations highlights a landscape combining Mediterranean evergreen elements and deciduous/wetland woods (notably oak, elm and alder), consistent with a lake-margin environment behind a coastal dune cordon. 

Bibliography: Marconi 2018 ; Manfredini (ed.) 2002.

contexts.name: Oak posts and postholes
contexts.description:
Charcoal recovered from the burnt posts associated with the hut’s postholes (both within the structure and along its perimeter) was identified as oak (Quercus sp.). This points to the deliberate selection of a hard, durable timber for the vertical load-bearing elements of the building (posts and principal supports), consistent with the need to anchor the roof and withstand long-term structural stress.

Bibliography: Celant, De Santis, Merlo & De Grossi Mazzorin 1998, Una casa dell’età del Ferro: la capanna di Fidene; “Una capanna dell’età del Ferro: archeologia sperimentale a Fidene”, Scuole Musei in Comune Roma (web resource).

contexts.name: Walkway
contexts.description:
Wood remains attributed to horizontal components—explicitly including the walkway/boarding set on the bench in front of the entrance—were identified as elm (Ulmus sp.). In the publication this is interpreted as a functional choice: elm is described as comparably resistant but more flexible than oak, making it well suited to elements that had to “work” under movement and bending (walkways, boards, and other horizontals).

Bibliography: Celant, De Santis, Merlo & De Grossi Mazzorin 1998, Una casa dell’età del Ferro: la capanna di Fidene; “Una capanna dell’età del Ferro: archeologia sperimentale a Fidene”, Scuole Musei in Comune Roma (web resource).
